69Business Continuity Planning: 
Strengthening Organisational Resilience
Gujarat Mineral Development Corporation Ltd. (GMDC), a 
cornerstone of Gujarat’ s industrial and mineral resource 
development for over ﬁve decades, recognises that 
operational resilience is fundamental to sustaining its 
position as a trusted enterprise and value creator for its 
stakeholders. In line with this commitment, GMDC has 
instituted a comprehensive Business Continuity 
Management (BCM) framework, aligned with the principles 
of ISO 22301, to identify potential threats, assess their 
impact on business operations, and build the 
organisational capability required for an eﬀective and 
timely response .
For GMDC, business continuity extends beyond crisis 
response — it encompasses the resilience of its people , 
processes, premises, service providers, technology 
infrastructure , and the integrity and availability of critical 
information. This holistic approach ensures that, in the face 
of disruption, the Corporation remains equipped to 
safeguard its workforce , protect its reputation and brand 
equity , and preserve the continuity of its value-generating 
activities.
As part of this initiative , dedicated Business Continuity 
Plans have been developed across GMDC’ s key functions 
— including Mining and Power Operations, Finance, 
Marketing and Sales, Human Resources, Safety, 
Information Technology, Procurement, Legal and 
Compliance , and other critical departments — each integral 
to the Corporation ’s day-to-day operations and long-term 
strategic objectives. Given their respective roles in 
operational delivery, risk management, and decision-
support, ensuring the uninterrupted functioning of these departments is essential to GMDC’ s broader operational, 
ﬁnancial, and reputational stability .
Objectives
Each department’ s Business Continuity Plan is anchored on 
three core objectives — safeguarding the safety and 
security of employees and stakeholders during disruptive 
events; ensuring the recovery and resumption of critical 
activities within predeﬁned Recovery Time Objectives 
(RTOs); and minimising the adverse impact of disruptions 
across interdependent departments and processes.
Scope of the Plan
Each departmental Plan establishes a structured 
framework covering recovery strategies for critical 
activities, identiﬁcation of resources required for 
restoration, clearly assigned roles and responsibilities for 
key stakeholders, prioritised recovery of critical technology 
systems within agreed timelines, and provisioning of 
essential materials at designated recovery sites — tailored 
to the speciﬁc functions and dependencies of each 
department.
Through this structured and proactive approach to 
business continuity, GMDC continues to reinforce its 
commitment to organisational resilience across all 
functions — ensuring that critical operations remain 
uninterrupted, stakeholder interests are protected, and 
GMDC is well-positioned to navigate disruptions while 
sustaining long-term value creation.

16. INFORMATION  RELATED  TO TAX DEDUCTIBLE  AT 
SOURCE (TDS) / WITHHOLDING TAX ON DIVIDEND
 Pursuant to the provisions of the Income-tax Act, 2025, the 
Company is required to deduct tax at source ("TDS") / 
withhold tax at the prescribed rates from the dividend payable 
to its Members.
 The rate of TDS / withholding tax shall depend upon the 
residential status of the Member and the documents 
submitted by the Member with the Company, MCS Share 
Transfer Agent Limited ("RTA") or the Depository Participant, 
as applicable. Members are therefore requested to ensure 
that their Permanent Account Number (PAN), residential 
status, bank account details and other KYC particulars are 
updated with their respective Depository Participants, in case 
shares are held in dematerialised form, or with the Company's 
RTA, in case shares are held in physical form, on or before the 
Record Date.
 Resident Members who are eligible for non-deduction of tax 
or deduction of tax at a lower rate under the provisions of the 
Income-tax Act, 2025 are requested to submit the prescribed 
declarations, forms, certicates and other supporting 
documents, including Form 121 or certicate issued under 
Section  395(1)  of the Income-tax  Act, 2025,  wherever 
applicable, on or before 23rd September, 2026.
 Non-Resident Members, including Foreign Portfolio Investors 
(FPIs), Foreign Institutional Investors (FIIs) and other eligible 
Members, may avail the benet of the applicable Double 
Taxation Avoidance Agreement ("DTAA"), subject to 
submission of the prescribed documents, including Tax 
Residency Certicate, declaration in the prescribed form 
under the Income-tax Rules, 2026, declaration regarding 
benecial  ownership,  declaration  regarding  absence  of 
Permanent Establishment / Fixed Base in India and such 
other documents as may be prescribed under the Income-tax 
Act, 2025 and the Income-tax Rules, 2026, on or before 
23rd September, 2026.
 The Company shall determine the applicable TDS / 
withholding tax rate based on the documents available on 
record as on the Record Date and the documents received

 During the year, the Company strengthened its bauxite 
business through its Gadhsisa and Mevasa Bauxite Projects 
by adopting a customer-centric production strategy 
focussed on optimising both product quality and market 
demand. Production planning emphasized the desired 
grades of bauxite to meet customer requirements, while the 
production of various grade of bauxite was strategically 
moderated considering the existing inventory of bauxite and 
prevailing market demand. This approach enabled the 
Company to achieve a despatch volume of 4.87 lakh tonnes, 
generating H124 crore in revenue from its bauxite operations, 
making it the largest revenue contributor among the 
Company's non-lignite mining businesses.
 The strong performance was driven by several strategic 
initiatives, including scientic production planning, effective 
grade control, improvements in mining methodologies, and 
the implementation of mechanised mining operations. 
These initiatives were complemented by enhanced 
customer outreach, efcient inventory management, timely 
auction of low-grade bauxite, and the receipt of necessary 
approvals from the Government of Gujarat for the Gadhsisa 
and Mevasa projects. Operational efciencies were further 
strengthened through optimised stacking, systematic 
grading, and improved despatch planning, resulting in 
higher productivity, improved inventory turnover, and 
enhanced customer satisfaction.
 The Company also continued to strengthen its position in 
Gujarat's bauxite market by consistently supplying quality 
bauxite to key industries, including Refractory, Abrasives,

 4.6  Powering Progress: Power Generation
 Your Company’s power generation portfolio spans both 
thermal and renewable energy, with a total installed capacity 
of 456 MW. The Company operates the 250 MW lignite-

solar power assets spread across Gujarat. This diversied 
energy portfolio not only strengthens Gujarat's power supply 
but also demonstrates the Company’s commitment to a 
responsible and sustainable energy future

 4.4 Manganese
 Your Company continues to prioritize sustainability across 
its mining value chain by maximising the utilisation of 
available mineral resources. This strategic approach is 
focussed on enhancing resource efciency, minimizing 
wastage, and generating greater value from the Nation's 
nite geological reserves. By embracing the principles of the 
circular economy and optimising the utilisation of historical 
mining outputs, the Company is transforming previously 
underutilised resources into valuable commercial products.
 A notable example of this initiative is the strategic operational 
revival of the long-standing manganese project at 
Shivrajpur. Low-grade manganese dumps, which were 
historically categorised as mining waste, have been 
scientically evaluated, and supplied for value addition to 
downstream industrial consumers who convert into 
marketable mineral products, thereby ensuring optimal 
resource utilisation and reducing mineral wastage.
 As Manganese is recognised as a strategic mineral, this 
initiative not only promotes sustainable mining practices but 
also contributes to enhancing domestic resource security 
and supporting India's future mineral requirements.
 4.5 Silica Sand Business - A Landmark Growth Story
 FY 2025-26 marked a transformational year for your  
Company’s Silica Sand business at Rajpardi, recording the 
highest-ever annual despatch in the project's history. Driven 
by a focussed strategy of market expansion, new customer 
acquisition, and the consolidation of long-term supply 
arrangements, the business delivered an unprecedented 
growth trajectory that signicantly exceeded its annual 
targets.
 During the year, the business achieved a total despatch of 
20.91 lakh MT against an annual target of 13.00 lakh MT - 
representing a despatch achievement of 161% of target and 
a 201% year-on-year increase over FY 2024-25 (6.94 lakh 
MT). Correspondingly, sales revenue surged from H10 crore 
in FY 2024-25 to H36 crore in FY 2025-26, reecting a growth 
of 260% and demonstrating successful monetisation of the 
Company’s available mineral resources. Notably, the 
Rajpardi Project achieved operational breakeven during the 
year -  a signicant nancial milestone.
 This exceptional performance was underpinned by 
deliberate strategic initiatives. The customer base was 
strengthened through the enrolment of six new Long-Term 
Supply (LTS) customers via the Expression of Interest (EOI) 
process, while additional quantities were successfully 
allotted to established customers, enabling higher despatch 
volumes. The Long-Term Supply model proved particularly 
effective, ensuring consistent and committed offtake that 
provided operational stability and revenue predictability 
throughout the year. 
 The cumulative impact of these initiatives was substantial. 
GMDC successfully transitioned the Rajpardi Silica Sand 
business from a traditional, transactional sales approach to 
a customer-centric, market-driven model-one characterised 
by stable long-term partnerships and proactive demand 
management. The establishment of a strong, diversied LTS Mine District Production / Generation (MU)

 6.3 Ambaji Copper Project - Unlocking Gujarat's Metal 
Potential
 In FY 2025-26, your Company has made signicant process 
in operationalising its copper project near Ambaji in 
Banaskantha, with exploration completed over 184-hectare 
area. This project is among the richest globally in metal 
concentration and also with over drilling of ~24,900 mtr, 
your company has successfully augmented resources from 
~10 million tonnes to ~11.3 million tonnes.
 Further strengthening the project’s advancement, key 
statutory approvals were secured during FY 2025-26. 
These include the Mining Plan approval obtained in July 
2025 and the Wildlife Conservation Plan approval granted in 
January 2026, marking critical milestones toward project 
development and operational-readiness.
 A beneciation plant is proposed to recover multiple metal 
streams for electronics, transport, clean energy, and export 
markets. With stakeholder engagement for pre-feasibility 
studies underway, the project marks your Company’s 
formal entry into non-ferrous mining, aligned with India’s 
Atmanirbhar Bharat vision in strategic metals.
 6.4 New Lignite Projects - Extending your Company’s 
Lignite Leadership
 To ensure long-term lignite availability and replace 
depleting legacy mines, your Company undertook its most 
ambitious lignite expansion comprising six new mining 
projects across Kutch and South Gujarat. These include 
Lakhpat Punhrajpur, Panandhro Extension, Bharkandam, 
Ghala, EFG Valia, and Damlai, collectively adding 482.9 
million tonnes of reserves to Gujarat’s energy supply base.
 In the year FY2025-26, your Company has achieved a key 
milestone with the grant of Environmental Clearance (EC) 
for the Lakhpat Punhrajpur Project. Notably, this is the rst 
mine in India to receive EC for the simultaneous extraction 
of two major minerals, lignite and limestone, marking a 
signicant regulatory and operational advancement. The 
ground breaking of Lakhpat Punhrajpur Project has been 
done in June,  2026.
 All mines are at various stages of implementation, with 
mining contracts awarded, land acquisition underway, and 
phased development aligned with environmental 
protocols. This lignite pipeline will serve Gujarat’s MSME 
sector, reduce dependence on imported coal, and 
strengthen your Company’s role as a key contributor to the 
state’s energy resilience.

 During the year, your Company progressed on developing a

gasication. In parallel, pre-feasibility studies have been

Coal Block (Odisha) and lignite gasication at the EFG Valia 
and Ghala Lignite Blocks (Gujarat).

6.  EMERGING STRATEGIC HORIZONS
 6.1 Rare Earth Elements - Mining for a Self-Reliant India
 Your Company’s Kadipani Rare Earth Project is a 
strategically signicant initiative aligned with India’s vision 
of self-reliance in critical minerals and strengthening 
domestic supply chains for green energy, defence, 
electronics, and advanced manufacturing sectors. Located 
in Chhota Udepur district, the deposit is one of the largest 
identied hard-rock rare earth resources in India and is 
expected to support the country’s growing rare earth 
requirements.
 During the year, key milestones were achieved with the 
approval of the Mining Plan and Mine Closure Plan by the 
Atomic Minerals Directorate for Exploration and Research 
(AMD). Your Company has also acquired indigenous rare 
earth processing technology developed by BARC and is 
establishing analytical, bench-scale, and pilot-scale 
processing facilities at iCEM to build in-house capabilities 
across the value chain. In addition, plans for a Rare Earth 
Hub at Bharuch have progressed, along with stakeholder 
engagement at domestic and international levels to explore 
collaboration opportunities.
 Your Company also signed an MoU with NMDC dated on 
16.03.2026, MoU was signed in the Rare Earth Elements 
(REE) sector, the main purpose of which is to examine the 
feasibility of developing an integrated rare earth value chain 
in the state of Gujarat.
 Going forward, your Company will focus on securing 
remaining statutory clearances, advancing mine 
development, commissioning pilot-scale facilities, and 
validating processing technology for commercial 
deployment. Parallel efforts will continue to establish 
downstream processing and manufacturing capabilities, 
positioning Gujarat as a key hub in India’s emerging rare 
earth ecosystem and supporting the national objective of 
Aatmanirbhar Bharat.
 6.2 Limestone - Cementing your Company’s Industrial 
Legacy:
 Your Company holds three greeneld lignite blocks in 
Western Kutch, Gujarat, underlain by an estimated 2.5 
billion tonnes of cement-grade limestone one of the largest 
such reserves in India. As part of its strategic diversication, 
your Company aims to monetise this resource in three 
phases over the next 3–5 years: Lakhpat Punhrajpur (Wave 
I), Panandhro Extension (Wave II), and Bharkandam (Wave 
III). In Wave I, your Company offered 800 million tonnes 
through an EOI and competitive bidding process, 
culminating in the selection of three companies. Your 
company has entered into long-term supply agreements 
with  identied partners. These initiatives are part of your 
Company’s vision to transform Western Kutch into a major 
cement production hub, leveraging its coastal advantage, 
market access, and efcient logistics. The initiative is 
expected to spur industrial development, attract

 Going forward, your Company will focus on assessing the

 6.6 From Gujarat to Odisha - your Company’s Strategic 
Coal Footprint
 As part of its strategic diversication into coal mining, the 
Company holds signicant coal block allocations in the 
state of Odisha. The Burapahar Block, situated in 
Sundaragada district, holds geological reserves of 548 
million tonnes, while the Baitarni (West) Block in Anugola 
district holds geological reserves of 1,097 million tonnes. 
Together, these two blocks represent a combined 
geological resource base of approximately 1,645 million 
tonnes, with mineable reserves estimated at around 660 
million tonnes. Upon full ramp-up, the combined 
production capacity from these blocks is expected to 
exceed 20 million tonnes per annum (MTPA), marking a 
transformational step in the Company's long-term 
operational strategy.
 In addition to the above, the Company has executed a Coal 
Mining Development and Production Agreement (CMDPA) 
with the Ministry of Coal for the Kudanali-Lubri Coal Mine, 
which carries a geological resource of 396.10 million metric 
tonnes (MMT). This agreement further reinforces the 
Company’s expanding footprint in the national coal sector.
 During the nancial year 2025-26, signicant progress was 
achieved in respect of the Baitarni (West) Block, with 
meaningful advancements made in land acquisition, mine 
plan approvals, and the obtainment of requisite statutory 
clearances. These developments are expected to 
accelerate the timelines for commencement of mining 
operations at this block.
 Beyond its mining operations, your Company has also 
established a meaningful Corporate Social Responsibility 
(CSR) presence in Odisha. A school has been set up to 
serve the needs of local communities in the project-affected 
areas, with further plans underway for the establishment of 
a hospital and a sports academy, reecting the Company's 
commitment to inclusive and sustainable development.
 On the utilisation front, your Company has forged a strategic 
partnership with Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Limited 
(GUVNL), under which coal sourced from the Odisha 
blocks will be utilised to support 4,400 MW of thermal power 
generation capacity. An additional 1,000 MW of generation 
capacity is also envisaged to be met through coal 
production from the Company's upcoming Gujarat lignite 
mines, thereby strengthening the energy security 
framework of the state of Gujarat.

 During the year, the Company continued to invest

Company’s ambitious growth agenda in the years ahead.
 On the safety training front, Extended Reality (XR)-based

consciousness across the Company’s mine sites.

 The Company has in place a robust system of Internal

 24.3 Water Stewardship and Resource Conservation
 Recognising water as a critical natural resource, your 
Company strengthened its water stewardship practices 
across its operations. At the thermal power plant, the 
Company implemented an internal recycling system that 
reuses around 80 cubic metres of RO reject water per day, 
thereby reducing wastewater discharge and improving 
overall water efciency. During the year, the Company 
treated and utilised 5,12,616 cubic metres of pit water 
through its Efuent Treatment Plant (ETP) and RO facilities. 
In addition, the Company installed a 25 cubic metres per 
day Sewage Treatment Plant (STP), with treated 
wastewater being used for gardening and greenbelt 
development. Rainwater conservation measures were also 
implemented across operational areas.
 24.4 Waste to Resource and Circular Economy
 Following circular economy principles, your Company 
transformed industrial byproducts and scrap materials into 
usable assets. Fly ash generated at the thermal power 
station was converted into construction materials through 
an automated brick manufacturing facility producing 
approximately 1,000–1,500 bricks per day. Scrap material 
was repurposed into functional infrastructure through in-
house fabrication.
 24.5 Renewable Energy and Clean Energy Transition
 By installing a total of 170 kW of solar power plants, 
including rooftop plants, parking shadow solar systems, 
and lighting infrastructure, at Gadhsisa, Umarsar, 
Bhavnagar and Mevasa Projects, the Company expanded 
its clean energy initiatives. Rooftop solar power produced 
approximately 2,22,984 kWh of clean energy, while the 5 
MW solar power plant produced 626,520 kWh of electricity.
 24.6 Air Pollution Control & Monitoring
 Your Company invested in advanced monitoring and digital 
technologies, including the installation of three 24×7 
Continuous Ambient Air Quality Monitoring Stations 
(CAAQMS). Together with dry fog systems, water sprinkling 
arrangements and sprinkler systems along 7 km of haul 
routes, these measures strengthened emissions 
compliance and environmental performance.
 24.7 Sustainability Commitment
 The Company's sustainability journey reects its 
commitment to regulatory excellence and its intent to 
support India’s transition towards a resilient, low-carbon, 
and environmentally responsible economy. Your  
Company remains committed to creating enduring 
environmental and social value through responsible mining 
practices, innovation-driven sustainability solutions, and a 
balanced approach to economic growth, ecological 
preservation, and community well-being.

Conservation of Energy, Technology Absorption and Foreign Exchange Earnings

A.  CONSERVATION OF ENERGY
(i)  Steps Taken or Impact on Conservation of Energy
The Company has been consistently endeavouring to strengthen its energy conservation framework across all its operational sites and 
administrative establishments. During the nancial year 2025-26, GMDC has undertaken several measures aimed at reducing energy 
consumption and improving overall energy efciency.
The key steps undertaken in this regard include:
• Installation of Solar Rooftop Systems: Solar rooftop systems have been planned for installation at Bhavnagar (50 KW) and Mevasa (25 
KW), as well as at other buildings, ofces, and townships across various GMDC project locations. Financial and technical analysis for 
these installations has been completed, and site visits have been conducted. The projects are presently at the implementation/approval 
stage.
• Optimisation of Existing Solar Infrastructure: The 5 MW Solar Power Plant at Panandhro is being optimised through the replacement 
of 250 KW solar modules. Financial and technical analysis has been completed, and the proposal is at the nalisation/implementation 
planning stage, which is expected to enhance the generation efciency of the existing plant.
• Reactive Power Management: A 100 KVAR capacitor bank has been installed at the 5 MW Solar Power Plant, with the objective of 
reducing reactive power losses and improving the power factor of the plant. This initiative was completed in May 2026 and is expected to 
result in tangible savings in energy loss.
• Transmission Infrastructure Upgradation: Replacement work of the conductor, earthwire, and associated hardware on the 66 kV D/C 
Madhavpur–Gorsar transmission line is in progress. Payment has been made by GMDC, and GETCO is in the process of preparing the 
Request for Proposal (RFP) to oat the tender.
• Solar Feasibility Assessment at Gadhsisha Mines: A feasibility study is presently underway to assess the potential for solar and wind 
power generation across the group of mines at Gadhsisha. Land parcel analysis is ongoing and ndings are expected to facilitate 
informed investment decisions in renewable energy for this cluster.
• Solar Installation at LTPS Township: Exploration of solar energy installation at the LTPS township is ongoing, with load analysis 
presently in progress. The project is awaiting auxiliary load data to proceed with detailed planning.
(ii)  Steps Taken by the Company for Utilising Alternate Sources of Energy
GMDC has made signicant strides in diversifying its energy portfolio towards renewable and alternate energy sources, in alignment with the 
Government of Gujarat's broader energy transition objectives. The key initiatives undertaken by the Company during FY 2025-26 are as 
follows:
• Wind Power Operations: The Company continues to operate wind power projects at various locations. As part of efforts to enhance the 
safety and operational efciency of these assets, climbing systems have been installed at 67 wind turbines across multiple wind power 
project sites. Work orders for the same were issued and installation was completed in January 2026.
• Hybrid Renewable Energy Project in Partnership with GACL: The Company has entered into a strategic partnership with Gujarat 
Alkalies and Chemicals Limited (GACL) for the development of a hybrid renewable energy project (combining solar and wind) to cater to 
the power requirements of GACL. A Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) has been signed between the two entities. Draft 
documentation including the Request for Proposal (RFP), Shareholders' Agreement (SHA), and Power Conversion Agreement (PCA) 
has been prepared. Discussions on the nalisation of the RFP are currently in progress.
• Solar Rooftop and Ground-Mounted Projects: As stated above, rooftop solar installations are being planned at multiple GMDC 
establishments and project locations. These initiatives collectively reect the Company's commitment to progressively augmenting the 
share of clean energy in its overall energy mix.
(iii)  Capital Investment on Energy Conservation Equipments
During the nancial year 2025-26, the Company has made targeted capital investments towards energy conservation infrastructure, 
including the installation of the 100 KVAR capacitor bank at the 5 MW Solar Power Plant at Panandhro for reactive power management, and 
the payment made towards replacement of transmission line infrastructure. Further capital outlays towards rooftop solar projects and the 
solar module replacement programme at Panandhro are expected to be incurred upon completion of ongoing procurement and approval 
processes. Detailed breakup of such capital expenditure is maintained in the Company's nancial records.ANNEXURE IVEnabling Billion Dreams of Viksit Bharat
98
=== page 100 ===
B.  TECHNOLOGY ABSORPTION
(i)  Efforts Made Towards Technology Absorption
The Company continues to invest in the adoption and absorption of modern technologies relevant to its core operations in mining, power 
generation, and renewable energy. During the nancial year, the Company has focussed on the following technology-related initiatives:
• Adoption of advanced climbing and safety systems for wind turbines, ensuring improved operational reliability and maintenance 
efciency.
• Upgradation of the 5 MW Solar Power Plant at Panandhro through replacement of solar modules with higher-capacity units, leveraging 
the latest advancements in photovoltaic technology.
• Implementation of reactive power management technology through capacitor bank installation, optimising the performance of solar 
power infrastructure.
• Feasibility assessment of hybrid renewable energy technologies (solar-wind combination) for potential deployment at the Gadhsisa 
mines cluster.
• Deployed IIoT sensors across key mining equipment to capture real-time data on engine hours, idle time, fuel consumption, and asset 
movement.
• Implemented centralised monitoring dashboards for continuous performance tracking, automated alerts, and contractor-level 
benchmarking.
• Introduced idle time optimisation measures through data-driven operational control.
• Adopted IoT-enabled GPS tracking and location intelligence systems across excavation and hauling eets.
• Enabled real-time route optimisation and dynamic mapping to minimise lead distances and improve eet efciency.
• Utilised advanced analytics for fuel consumption monitoring and optimisation across operations.
(ii)  Benets Derived
The technology absorption and adoption efforts undertaken by the Company are expected to yield the following benets:
• Improved energy generation efciency at the Panandhro Solar Power Plant, resulting in higher output from the same installed capacity.
• Reduction in reactive power losses and improvement in power factor at solar power assets, leading to cost savings.
• Enhanced safety and longevity of wind turbine assets through adoption of modern climbing and maintenance systems.
• Long-term cost reduction through progressive substitution of grid power with captive renewable energy generation at Company 
establishments.
• Achieved 12–15% reduction in idle time, leading to signicant savings in diesel consumption.
• Reduced fuel wastage through improved operational efciency and equipment utilisation.
• Lowered energy consumption (diesel) by optimising haul routes and reducing unnecessary travel distances.
• Improved equipment utilisation levels (60–65%), reducing excess fuel usage.
• Generated fuel cost savings of H49 per tonne (idle time reduction) and INR 85 per tonne (improved utilisation).
• Achieved additional savings of H144 per tonne through lead distance optimisation, directly reecting reduced fuel usage.
• Demonstrated large-scale energy savings potential (H 200–250 crore annually) through resource and fuel efciency improvements.
• Contributed to overall reduction in carbon footprint and enhanced energy efciency in mining operations.
(iii)  Imported Technology
During the last three years reckoned from the beginning of the nancial year 2025-26, the Company has not imported any technology. 
Accordingly, the disclosures required under sub-clauses (a), (b), (c), and (d) of Rule 8(3)(B)(iii) are not applicable.
(iv)  Expenditure Incurred on Research and Development
During the year, the Company incurred H12,14,450 (0.0046% of turnover) on R&D activities, primarily towards gasication and adoption of 
advanced technologies aimed at improving operational and environmental performance.

integrated waste management, and the benecial use of overburden for

4. Does the entity have an anti-corruption or anti-bribery policy? If yes, provide details in brief and if available, provide a web-
link to the policy.
Yes. GMDC has established a comprehensive framework to prevent and address corruption and bribery, embedded within its Code of 
Conduct for Directors and Senior Management and Code of Conduct for Employees. These Codes dene clear standards of ethical and 
professional behaviour and prohibit the offering, giving, soliciting, or accepting of bribe, kickbacks, facilitation payments, or any form of 
undue nancial or non-nancial advantage. They also prohibit the misuse of position, conicts of interest, and attempts to inuence 
decision-making through improper means, while mandating compliance with applicable laws, including the Prevention of Corruption 
Act, 1988, and promoting transparency and accountability in all business dealings, including procurement and stakeholder interactions. 
This framework is further reinforced through a structured a vigil mechanism that provides secure channels for reporting concerns related 
to corruption, fraud, or unethical conduct. It enables the escalation of matters to appropriate authorities, including the Vigilance 
Department and the Audit Committee, while ensuring protection against retaliation for individuals reporting in good faith. The 
mechanism is supported by internal audits, vigilance oversight, and periodic sensitisation programmes which collectively strengthen 
governance, risk management, and ethical conduct across the organisation. 
The relevant policies are available on the Company’s website: Corporate Policies Corporate Policies GMDC - Gujarat Mineral

2. Does the entity have processes in place to avoid/ manage conict of interests involving members of the Board? (Yes/No) If 
Yes, provide details of the same.
Yes. GMDC has established robust processes to identify, prevent, and manage conicts of interest involving Board members through its 
Code of Conduct for Directors and Senior Management. The Code requires Directors and Senior Management personnel to act in the 
best interests of the Company, exercise independent judgement, and disclose any actual or potential conicts of interest in a timely 
manner. Such disclosures are submitted to the Company Secretary for review and approval before the relevant matter is undertaken. 
In addition, the Related Party Transaction Policy provides a structured framework for identifying, reviewing, approving, and monitoring 
transactions that may involve potential conicts of interest. Such transactions are evaluated to ensure they are conducted on an arm’s-
length basis and in the ordinary course of business, with oversight from the appropriate governance bodies, including the Audit 
Committee, wherever applicable. These mechanisms promote transparency, accountability, and adherence to sound corporate 
governance practices.

PRINCIPLE 2: Businesses should provide goods and services in a manner that is sustainable and safe
At GMDC, operations are undertaken with a strong emphasis on safety, sustainability, and environmental stewardship. Mining activities 
are planned and executed to ensures safe resource extraction while minimising the impact on land, water resources, biodiversity, and 
surrounding communities. The Company integrates sustainable practices across the entire mining lifecycle, supported by efcient 
technologies, responsible waste management, and strict adherence to applicable environmental and statutory requirements. This 
approach enables GMDC to promote responsible while ensuring operational safety and long-term sustainability.

2. a. Does the entity have procedures in place for sustainable sourcing? (Yes/No)
 Yes. GMDC has established procedures for sustainable sourcing through a comprehensive procurement framework governed by a 
formal procurement policy applicable to the procurement of materials, services, consultancy engagements, and infrastructure 
requirements. Procurement activities are primarily carried out through the Government e Marketplace (GeM) platform, along with 
other transparent mechanisms such as  e-tendering, competitive bidding, and RFP processes. This framework ensures 
transparency, regulatory compliance, and a clear audit trail for all procurement transactions.
 As part of its responsible sourcing approach, GMDC integrates ESG considerations into its vendor selection and assessment 
processes. Parameters such as environmental compliance, occupational health and safety standards, labour practices, and ethical 
conduct are incorporated into vendor assessments. Due diligence is conducted prior to onboarding, and entities do not meet 
statutory, environmental, or ethical requirements may be disqualied or blacklisted in accordance with the procurement policy.
 Additionally, GMDC encourages local sourcing wherever operationally feasible, helping to minimise logistics related emissions while 
contributing to regional economic development. The consistent application of sustainability criteria across procurement categories 
enables the Company to maintain responsible, transparent, and environmentally conscious sourcing practices.

At GMDC, emphasis is placed on safeguarding the well-being, safety, and dignity of our workforce, including contract workers and value

In addition, GMDC continuously strengthens fair labour practices and promote human rights awareness among contract workers and

6. Is there a mechanism available to receive and redress grievances for the following categories of employees and workers? If 
yes, give details of the mechanism in brief.
Yes/No (If Yes, then give details of the mechanism in brief)
Yes. GMDC has established a formal grievance redressal framework supported by 
dened organisational processes, and guided by the principles of transparency and 
accountability, including alignment with the Right to Information Act, 2005. 
Grievance Redressal Committees are constituted at both corporate and project levels to 
ensure the fair and timely resolution of concerns. Employees and workers may raise 
grievances through multiple channels, including site HR teams, grievance boxes, and 
direct reporting to supervisors. 
The framework is further supported by an HR Sub-Committee and includes provisions 
to address concerns of persons with disabilities. A dedicated Internal Committee under 
the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) 
Act, 2013 (POSH), is also in place to address complaints related to harassment.
Additional mechanisms include appellate processes for performance evaluations 
through an Appellate Committee. In disciplinary matters, representation may be made 
before the presenting ofcer, with provisions for further appeal to higher authorities. 
Where appropriate, unresolved matters may be pursued through legal channels, 
including the High Court. Support is also available under the Equal Opportunity Policy in 
accordance with the RPWD Act, 2016, as well as through the HR Department for general 
concerns. As a Government Company, GMDC also provides access to additional 
grievance redressal forums within the government system. These mechanisms operate 
in accordance with applicable legal requirements and organisational policies, ensuring 
fairness, transparency, accountability, and inclusivity across the organisation.Permanent Workers

10. Health and safety management system:
a. Whether an occupational health and 
safety management system has been 
implemented by the entity? (Yes/ No). 
If yes, the coverage such system?Yes. GMDC has implemented a comprehensive Occupational Health and Safety 
(OHS) Management System across its mining sites and administrative operations. 
The system covers both employees and contract workers and includes safety 
governance, hazard identication, risk control procedures, mandatory training, 
audits, and emergency preparedness measures. OHS practices are aligned with 
applicable statutory requirements under the Mines Act, 1952, Mines Rules, 1955, 
and Mines Vocational Training Rules, 1966, ensuring regulatory compliance and 
worker health and safety. Site-level Safety Committees have been established to 
regularly monitor, review, and strengthen health and safety performance across 
operations.
b. What are the processes used to 
identify work-related hazards and 
assess risks on a routine and non-
routine basis by the entity?GMDC follows structured and site specic processes to identify work related 
hazards and assess risk. These include Hazard Identication and Risk Assessment 
(HIRA), job safety analyses (JSA) for task specic risks, and dedicated 
assessments for non-routine or high risk operations. These activities are supported 
by pre task safety briengs and a permit-to-work (PTW) system for critical 
operations. Continuous oversight is maintained by supervisors and safety ofcers, 
through periodic inspections, safety audits and internal reviews, as dened in the 
Company’s Safety Manual.

including fractures to the left hip and left orbit, after falling from a truck while covering a tarpaulin near the weighbridge. As the 
individual was neither a GMDC employee nor a contractor engaged by GMDC, there was no loss of man-hours to the Company, and

12.  Describe the measures taken by the entity to ensure a safe and healthy workplace.
 GMDC ensures a safe and healthy workplace through a structured Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) Management System and 
a comprehensive Safety Management Plan, implemented across all mining sites and administrative ofces and applicable to both 
employees and contractual personnel. These systems operate within the Company’s integrated QHSE framework and are aligned 
with statutory requirements under the Mines Act, 1952, Mines Rules, 1955, and Mines Vocational Training Rules, 1966, as well as the 
requirements of ISO 45001 under the integrated iQEHS management systems.
 Workplace risks are systematically managed through structured hazard identication and task-based risk assessments, including 
Job Safety Analysis (JSA) for critical activities, supported by advanced monitoring systems such as slope stability radar at mining 
sites. The Company enforces the mandatory use of appropriate PPE, with continuous oversight by designated safety personnel to 
ensure adherence across operations. Regular safety training programmes, mock drills, and clearly-dened emergency response 
and evacuation procedures are conducted to enhance preparedness, supported by on-site rst-aid facilities and availability of 
ambulances in accordance with statutory requirements. In addition, periodic health check-ups are conducted for the workforce, 
while health and safety performance is closely monitored through site-level safety committees, internal reviews, and external audits 
under QEHS protocols. Collectively, these measures enable GMDC to maintain a proactive, compliant, and robust safety culture 
across its operations.

15.  Provide details of any corrective action taken or underway to address safety-related incidents (if any) and on signicant risks 
/ concerns arising from assessments of health & safety practices and working conditions.
 Safety incidents and risks identied through assessments at GMDC are managed through a structured Corrective and Preventive 
Action (CAPA) framework. Incidents and observations are investigated to determine their root causes, followed by the 
implementation of corrective measures, including revisions to procedure, strengthened safety controls, engineering interventions, 
and targeted training programmes.
 A fatal incident involving outsourced height-based maintenance work was investigated at the corporate level. Based on the ndings, 
corrective and preventive measures were implemented to address identied gaps and strengthen safety governance. Key actions 
included classifying work at height and conned space activities as high-risk tasks, along with the mandatory barricading or fencing 
of open edges, ducts, and fall-prone areas. Enhanced fall-protection measures, including the use of appropriate PPE, lifelines, 
guardrails, and strict supervision, have also been enforced.
 Additional measures included mandatory medical examinations for personnel engaged in hazardous activities, the development of 
Safe Operating Procedures (SOPs) in local languages, and strengthened contractor oversight through routine inspections by safety 
ofcers and site personnel. The Hazard Identication and Risk Assessment (HIRA) framework was updated to incorporate clearly  
dened controls, responsibilities, and escalation protocols. Safety guidelines for outsourced activities were formalised, covering 
regulatory compliance, manpower deployment, training, Job Safety Analysis (JSA), and toolbox talks.
 High-risk activities are now subject to enhanced monitoring through periodic inspections and compliance checks. Corrective actions 
are reviewed by cross-functional teams, with the implementation is tracked to ensure timely closure. Learnings are shared across 
locations to prevent recurrence, with the effectiveness is periodically reviewed through safety committee meetings, inspections, and 
QEHS audits to support continuous improvement.

2. Provide the measures undertaken by the entity to ensure that statutory dues have been deducted and deposited by the 
value chain partners.
 The Company has implemented a robust governance and oversight framework to ensure that statutory dues are deducted and 
deposited by its value chain partners. Following steps are followed:
 Step 1: Due Diligence and Onboarding:  Value chain partners are selected through a structured due diligence process that 
evaluates their statutory compliance track record, nancial standing, and adherence to applicable legal requirements, 
including past compliance with statutory deductions and remittances.
 Step 2: Contractual Compliance Requirements:  All contracts explicitly incorporate clauses mandating compliance with 
applicable labour and statutory laws, including timely deduction and deposit of dues such as provident fund, ESI and other 
applicable contributions. These requirements form an integral part of the contractual obligations.
 Step 3: Monitoring, Verication, and Audits:  Compliance by value chain partners is monitored through periodic reviews, audits, 
and verication of statutory records and ling. Supporting documents are examined, and any non-conformities identied is 
addressed through corrective action and follow-up mechanisms.
 Step 4: Periodic Declarations and Enforcement:  Value chain partners are required to submit periodic compliance declarations 
along with documentary evidence of statutory payments. Continued engagement is linked to satisfactory compliance, and 
instances of non-compliance may result in to penalties, withholding of payments, or disqualication/ blacklisting, as per 
applicable policies.

1. Provide the processes for consultation between stakeholders and the Board on economic, environmental, and social topics 
or if consultation is delegated, how is feedback from such consultations provided to the Board.
 GMDC has institutionalised a structured governance framework to facilitate stakeholder consultation on economic, environmental, 
and social matters, and to ensure that stakeholder perspectives is effectively integrated into decision-making at the Board- level. 
The Company follows a systematic multi-step stakeholder engagement process that includes stakeholder identication and 
mapping, prioritisation based on inuence and impact, and the implementation of tailored engagement mechanisms suited to 
different stakeholder groups.
 Stakeholder consultations are carried out through formal and transparent channels, such as public hearings, community 
consultations, investor briengs, vendor forums, and grievance redressal mechanisms. The feedback received through these 
engagements is systematically captured, analysed, and evaluated by relevant functional teams to identify material issues, 
emerging concerns, risks, and stakeholder expectations.
 The insights generated are periodically consolidated and escalated to senior management and relevant Board committees, 
through structured reports, sustainability reviews, and compliance updates. This enables the Board to exercised informed oversight 
on ESG-related matters and ensures that stakeholder perspectives are incorporated into strategic planning, risk mitigation, and 
policy formulation. Where direct consultation with the Board does not occur, the governance framework ensures that stakeholder 
inputs are routed through established management process, providing a clear linkage between stakeholder engagement and 
Board-level decision-making.
 This approach supports continuous improvement and ensures that stakeholder expectations are embedded within the Company’s 
ESG priorities, sustainability roadmap, and long-term value creation strategy, reinforcing transparency, accountability, and 
responsible business conduct.
2. Whether stakeholder consultation is used to support the identication and management of environmental and social topics 
(Yes / No). If so, provide details of instances as to how the inputs received from stakeholders on these topics were 
incorporated into policies and activities of the entity.
 Yes. GMDC actively leverages stakeholder consultations to identify, assess, and manage environmental and social topics across its 
operations, and to integrate stakeholder inputs into policies, programmes, and operational practices.
 As part of the regulatory framework, public hearings are conducted during the Environmental Clearance (EC) process for mining 
and industrial projects. These hearings, facilitated by the respective State Pollution Control Boards and conducted in the presence 
of district authorities, provide a formal platform for local communities to raise environmental and social concerns. Issues highlighted 
during these hearings are formally recorded, evaluated, and addressed through appropriate measures, with periodic compliance 
reports submitted to regulatory authorities.
 Beyond statutory requirements, GMDC undertakes continuous stakeholder engagement through dedicated CSR teams deployed 
at project locations, enabling direct interaction with local communities, village representatives and other stakeholders. Feedback 
received through engagements is incorporated into programme design and implementation, ensuring that interventions remain 
responsive to local needs and priorities.
 Key initiatives undertaken include:
• Infrastructure Development:  GMDC has undertaken targeted infrastructure initiatives in water-scarce and underserved regions 
to support sustainable rural development. the construction of check dams has improved water availability and groundwater 
recharge, beneting domestic use and agricultural activities. The installation of solar-powered street lighting in remote villages 
has enhanced safety while reducing dependence on conventional energy sources. Additionally, the development of community 
halls, sheds, RCC roads, drainage systems, and paver block pathways has strengthened social infrastructure and improved all-
weather accessibility to schools, Anganwadis, and interior habitations.
• Education Support:  To promote access to quality education in remote areas, GMDC has established CBSE-afliated English-
medium schools at Nani Chher (Kutch) and Kadipani (Chhotaudepur) in collaboration with reputed institutions. The Company 
also supports government schools through the distribution of books and stationery. Scholarship programs for girl students are 
implemented to reduce dropout rates and encourage continued education. Further, initiatives such as sports activities and 
school transportation facilities in interior villages have contributed to improved enrolment, attendance, and overall student 
development.
• Health and Hygiene:  GMDC has strengthened access to healthcare by establishing hospitals in collaboration with Apollo 
Hospitals at Nani Chher and Kadipani, providing free and quality medical services, including OPD, specialised treatment, 
diagnostic services, pharmacy support and telemedicine facilities. To extend healthcare access to remote areas, mobile medical 
units conduct health check-ups, distribute medicines, and promote awareness on sanitation and preventive healthcare, 
beneting a large number of community members annually.
• Skill Development:  GMDC’s “Samarthya – Employment Oriented Skill Development Programme” focuses on improving 
enhancing the employability of among local youth through industry-relevant training delivered in collaboration with recognised 
partners. The programme covers diverse trades, such as CNC operations, solar installation, electrical work, warehousing, and 
healthcare assistance, thereby enabling sustainable livelihoods and contributing to local economic development.

PRINCIPLE 6: Businesses should respect and make efforts to protect and restore the environment
GMDC is committed to conducting its operations in an environmentally responsible manner by embedding sustainability considerations 
across its mining, mineral development, and power generation activities. The Company adopts a proactive approach to minimising 
environmental impact, optimising resource utilisation and promoting ecological restoration throughout the lifecycle of its operations. 
Key initiatives include improving energy efciency, adopting cleaner technologies such as coal gasication for sustainable utilisation of 
lignite, expanding renewable energy capacity, and gradual progressively electrifying operational equipment and eets to reduce 
emissions. GMDC also follows scientic overburden management and progressive mine reclamation practices, with a focus on land 
restoration, afforestation, and biodiversity conservation in and around its operational areas. Environmental considerations are 
integrated into operational planning through adherence to regulatory requirements, implementation of environmental management 
plans, and continuous monitoring mechanisms. Through these measures, GMDC aims to reduce its environmental footprint, enhance 
resource efciency, and contribute to long-term environmental sustainability, in alignment with national priorities relating to 
environmental protection and responsible mining.

5. Has the entity implemented a mechanism for Zero Liquid Discharge? If yes, provide details of its coverage and 
implementation.
 Yes. GMDC has implemented Zero Liquid Discharge (ZLD) systems across all of its mining sites as part of its commitment to 
sustainable water management. Wastewater generated from operations is treated through Efuent Treatment Plants (ETP) and 
Reverse Osmosis (RO) systems and is fully recycled and reused for non-potable purposes such as plantation, dust suppression, and 
other operational requirements. This closed-loop approach signicantly minimises freshwater consumption, eliminates the need for 
wastewater discharge, and promotes responsible water stewardship across operations.

10. Briey describe the waste management practices adopted in your establishments. Describe the strategy adopted by your 
company to reduce usage of hazardous and toxic chemicals in your products and processes and the practices adopted to 
manage such wastes.
 GMDC adopts structured and well-dened waste management practices across its mining and industrial operations, with a focus on 
resource optimisation, safe disposal, and environmental compliance. The primary waste generated from mining activities is 
overburden (OB), which is systematically managed through designated dumping areas and subsequently utilised for backlling and 
biological reclamation of mined-out areas. At newer mining locations, progressive mine closure practices are adopted, enabling 
implemented to enable concurrent reclamation and land restoration as mining activities advance.
 Fly ash generated from power plants is effectively utilised in mine restoration activities, reducing waste accumulation and supporting 
circular resource use. Additionally, the LTPS Plant operates as an in-house y ash brick manufacturing unit, with the produced bricks 
used for internal construction as well as supplied externally, promoting sustainable utilisation.
 Hazardous waste is managed in strict compliance with applicable regulatory requirements through authorised channels:
• Used oil and oil-contaminated waste are sent to certied recyclers or disposed of through MSTC.
• Bio-medical waste is handled through licensed disposal agencies.
• E-waste is centrally collected and routed to authorised recyclers.
• Battery waste is managed through buyback mechanism with approved vendors.
 Non hazardous waste, such as metal scrap is disposed of through buyback mechanisms using MSTC registered vendors, ensuring 
traceability and resource recovery.
 To minimise the use of hazardous and toxic materials, GMDC adopts process measures controlled material usage, and material 
substitution wherever feasible. The Company also ensures adherence to approved chemical usage protocols and applicable 
regulatory requirements across its operations. These practices collectively ensure reduction in hazardous waste generation, safe 
handling and disposal, and alignment with environmental sustainability objectives.

5. Does the entity have a business continuity and disaster management plan? Give details in 100 words/web link.
 Yes. GMDC has a Business Continuity and Disaster Management Plan in place to ensure operational resilience and safeguard 
employees, assets and surrounding communities during unforeseen events. The plan outlines protocols for emergency response, 
data recovery, and continuity of critical operations employees, assets, mining and power facilities. It also denes clear roles and 
responsibilities to enable timely coordination and response during emergencies. The framework is periodically reviewed and tested 
through mock drills to assess preparedness and improve effectiveness. These measures help minimises operational disruption, 
ensure safety, and maintain continuity of essential services, in compliance with statutory requirements.
6. Disclose any signicant adverse impact to the environment, arising from the value chain of the entity. What mitigation or 
adaptation measures have been taken by the entity in this regard?
 GMDC recognises that environmental impacts may arise across its value chain, particularly from activities such as mineral 
extraction, material handling, transportation, and contractor operations. The key environmental impacts identied include land 
disturbance, dust and air emissions, noise pollution, and water consumption. To mitigate these impacts, GMDC has implements 
the following measures:
•  Land management:  Progressive mine reclamation, afforestation, and green-belt development to address land disturbance 
and restore ecological balance.

•  Air and dust control:  Deployment of fog cannons, water sprinkling systems, covered material use of PUC-certied vehicles are

7. Percentage of value chain partners (by value of business done with such partners) that were assessed for environmental 
impacts. 
 Not Fully Assessed. GMDC ensures that its value chain partners comply with applicable environmental regulations through its 
structured procurement processes, including RFPs, tender conditions, and contractual provisions. Compliance with statutory 
environmental requirements forms a mandatory criterion during vendor selection and onboarding. However, comprehensive 
environmental impact assessments for all value chain partners have not yet been fully implemented. The Company is in the process 
of strengthening its supplier engagement framework and plans to introduce phased, formal ESG and environmental assessments

3. Describe the mechanisms to receive and redress grievances of the community.
 GMDC has implemented a structured grievance redressal mechanism to engage with communities across all operational locations 
and ensure timely resolution of concerns. Each project site is supported by a dedicated CSR team that serves as the primary 
interface with local communities. These teams maintain regular engagement with village representatives, Gram Panchayats and 
community groups to identify issues, address concerns, and facilitate prompt resolution.
 Grievances are received through multiple formal and informal channels, including community meetings, village-level consultations, 
and public hearings (as part of the Environmental Clearance process), and direct interactions with stakeholders. Additionally, 
village coordinators act as local representatives to enable continuous communication and escalation issues.
 All grievances are recorded, reviewed, and addressed in a time-bound manner in coordination with relevant departments. These 
mechanisms ensure transparency, accessibility, and responsiveness, and enable GMDC to effectively address community 
concerns while strengthening stakeholder trust and social licence to operate.

1. Describe the mechanisms in place to receive and respond to consumer complaints and feedback. 
 GMDC has implemented a structured, transparent, and multi channel mechanism to receive and respond to consumer complaints

logged, tracked, investigated, and resolved through documented procedures under the Quality Management System (QMS).
 Consumers can raise complaints through multiple accessible channels, including:
•   An online helpdesk on the Company’s website for complaint registration, categorisation, and document submission
•  Dedicated email support (contact@gmdcltd.com)
•   Telephone support through designated helpline numbers (079 27913501 / 27913200)
•   Statutory grievance platforms CPGRAMS, ensuring enhanced transparency and public accountability
 Complaints are routed to relevant departments and monitored by designated ofcials, ensuring accountability and timely 
resolution. A digital complaint management system and dashboard enable real-time tracking of complaints status, response 
timelines, and resolution outcomes, supporting effective monitoring and data-driven decision-making.
 GMDC also undertakes root cause analysis of complaints and implements appropriate corrective and preventive actions to 
minimise recurrence. Consumer communication is maintained throughout the process, ensuring timely updates and courteous 
handling of concerns.
Complaint and feedback data are periodically analysed to identify systemic issues and areas for improvement. Key learnings are 
integrated into SOPs, training programmes, and process enhancements, thereby strengthening service quality and consumer

5. Does the entity have a framework/ policy on cyber security and risks related to data privacy? (Yes/No) If available, provide a 
web-link of the policy.
 Yes. GMDC has established a comprehensive, layered, and risk-based framework to address cybersecurity and data privacy risks 
across its infrastructure, applications, cloud environments, and user systems. The framework is aligned with recognised industry 
standards and best practices and is supported by a combination of preventive, detective, and corrective controls.
 Key elements include robust network and perimeter security measures, such as rewalls, web application rewalls (WAF), 
advanced email security, sandboxing of uploaded les, and continuous monitoring of cloud environment. Endpoint and device 
security are strengthened through deployment of EDR/XDR solutions, Mobile Device Management (MDM), Cloud Access Security 
Broker (CASB) for SaaS applications, and regular system patching. The framework is further strengthened by threat detection and 
incident response mechanism including periodic vulnerability assessments and penetration testing (VAPT), centralised log 
monitoring, and proactive cybersecurity posture reviews. 
 GMDC also emphasises employee awareness and preparedness in managing cyber risks through regular cybersecurity 
awareness programmes and phishing simulations. In addition, business continuity and disaster recovery measures, including 
periodic drills, are implemented to ensure resilience and enable timely restoration of systems in the event of cyber incidents.
 Data privacy is addressed through controlled access protocols, secure congurations, monitoring systems, and incident response 
mechanisms to safeguard sensitive information. The Cybersecurity and Data Privacy policy is maintained as an internal governance 
document and is not currently available in the public domain.

Methodology
JointValues conducted this reasonable assurance engagement for the Company in accordance with the following standards issued by 
the International Auditing and Assurance Standards Board (IAASB):
• ISAE 3000 (Revised), Assurance Engagements Other Than Audits or Reviews of Historical Financial Information
• ISAE 3410, Assurance Engagements on Greenhouse Gas Statements
• JointValues conducted the engagement process with adherence to ethical requirements, professional standards, and compliance

Management for Firms that Perform Audits or Reviews of Financial Statements or Other Assurance or Related Services 
Engagement issued by IAASB.
• During the engagement, the assurance team complied with JointValues’s Code of Conduct, that denes independence and other 
ethical requirements and aligns with the best practices and the International Code of Ethics (ICE) for Professional Accountants 
(including International Independence Standards) issued by the International Ethics Standards Board for Accountants (IESBA).
Limitations and Exclusions
• Preparing the Company’s BRSR information requires management to set the criteria, decide what information is relevant to include, 
and make estimates and assumptions that impact the reported information.
• Reducing engagement risk to zero is rarely attainable; therefore, reasonable assurance is less than absolute assurance.
• Calculating and measuring certain amounts and BRSR Core metrics, such as GHG emissions, water, waste and energy footprint, 
involves assumptions/estimations and inherent measurement uncertainty. Even though we obtain sufcient appropriate evidence 
to support our opinion, it does not eliminate the uncertainty in these amounts and metrics.
• Evaluation, verication and assessment of any Company’s nancial performance and data have been out of the scope of this 
engagement, except relying on the Company’s third-party audited nancial reports as provided to us during the course of 
engagement, wherever materially required concerning the nine core attributes of the BRSR core. The assurance does not cover the 
Company’s statements that express opinions, claims, beliefs, aspirations, expectations, aims, or future intentions. Additionally, 
assertions related to Intellectual Property Rights and other competitive issues are beyond the scope of this assurance.
• Aspects of the BRSR and the data and information (qualitative or quantitative) as per BRSR Core attributes.

Procedures Followed
Given the circumstances of the engagement, in performing the engagement procedures, we have:
• Interacted with relevant personnel of Company’s management responsible for Sustainability, Environmental, Social and 
Governance (ESG) and their team through a combination of virtual meeting interactions at the Company’s corporate head ofce for 
understanding the process of collecting, collating the subject matter as per SEBI Circular for BRSR Core.
• Assessed the appropriateness of various assumptions, estimations and materiality thresholds used by the Company for data 
analysis.
• Performed analytical procedures to analyse trends in the historical data and accordingly ascertain the reasonableness of the data 
reported in the current year.
• Performed substantive testing on a sample basis of the identied sustainability indicators, to verify that the data had been 
appropriately measured with the underlying documents recorded, collated and reported, including returns and internal monitoring 
reports led to various authorities by the Company and relied upon by us. This includes assessing records and performing testing, 
including recalculation of sample data.

aspects of assurance. Our opinion on the continuing effectiveness of the Company’s internal controls is out of the scope of this

Responsibilities of Management at the Company
By publishing this assurance statement, the management of the Company acknowledges and understands that they are, inter-alia, 
responsible for the information provided in the BRSR for:
• Designing, implementing, and maintaining internal controls to ensure the information is free from material misstatement, including 
preventing deliberate misrepresentation.
• Selecting or establishing suitable criteria for preparing the information, considering applicable laws and regulations, identifying key 
aspects, engaging with stakeholders, and preparing and presenting the information according to the reporting criteria.
• Disclosing the applicable criteria used for preparation in the relevant report or statement.
• Preparing and calculating the information in accordance with the reporting criteria.
• Ensuring the reporting criteria are available to assurance providers and intended users with relevant explanations and 
assumptions.
• Establishing targets, goals, and performance measures and implementing actions to achieve them.
• Identifying and describing inherent limitations in measuring or evaluating information according to the reporting criteria.

REPORT ON CORPORATE GOVERNANCE
This Report on Corporate Governance for the nancial year ended March 31, 2026, prepared in accordance with Regulation 34(3) and 
Schedule V o f Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 (hereinafter 
referred to as “Listing Regulations/ LODR”).
1. COMPANY’S PHILOSOPHY ON CODE OF GOVERNANCE
Gujarat Mineral Development Corporation Limited (“GMDC/the Company”) demonstrates unwavering commitment to exemplary corporate 
governance principles across its entire value chain and all areas of its business operations. Our governance framework is built on the 
principles of transparency and proactive disclosure, ensuring that our operations align with the highest standards. As we navigate through 
an evolving energy and mineral landscape, we are consciously adopting agile and effective governance practices that mitigate risk and 
enhance operational excellence. Our philosophy remains clear: prioritising ethical leadership, maximise long-term value for our 
shareholders and contribute meaningfully to the socio-economic fabric of the nation.
Core Governance Values
The Company's governance philosophy is operationalised through the following core values:
i. Integrity: Integrity forms the bedrock of GMDC's operations and stakeholder relationships. We maintain the highest ethical standards 
in all business dealings, ensuring zero tolerance for corruption, fraud or malpractice.  
ii. Transparency: Transparency is central to GMDC's relationship with shareholders and the public. We believe that open, timely and 
accurate communication is essential for informed decision-making and building stakeholder condence.
iii. Accountability: Accountability at GMDC means clear ownership of decisions, actions and results at every organisational level. We 
have established robust mechanisms to ensure that responsibility is clearly dened and performance is rigorously evaluated.
iv. Responsibility: GMDC embraces responsibility that extends beyond legal compliance to encompass broader social, environmental 
and economic obligations. As a public sector undertaking, we recognise our dual mandate of commercial success and public welfare.
2. COMPLIANCE STATUS
 The Company has complied with all mandatory requirements of the Listing Regulations pertaining to Corporate Governance during 
FY 2025 -26 except otherwise stated in the Report. 
3. BOARD-OF-DIRECTORS
 i. Government Company
  GMDC is classied as a Government Company under Section 2(45) of the Companies Act, 2013 (“the Act”), with over 51% of its 
equity owned by the Government of Gujarat.
 ii. Appointment
  The power of appointment/reappointment of Directors on the Board, vests with the administrative department, i.e., Industry and 
Mines Department, Government of Gujarat.
 iii. Rotational Directors
  Directors are subject to retirement by rotation at the Annual General Meeting. Directors retiring under the rotation rule are eligible 
for reappointment in line with statutory requirements.
  Chairperson, Managing Director and Independent Directors are not liable to retire by rotation.
 iv. Board Composition
  As on March 31, 2026, the Board of the Company comprises individuals from diverse backgrounds, possessing a broad range of 
expertise, talent, experience, knowledge, and independence, with collective strengths spanning critical domains such as Public 
Policy & Governance, Finance & Accounts, Legal & Regulatory Affairs, and Strategic Management.
  The strength of the Board comprised 7 (seven) Directors as on March 31, 2026. More than half of the Board, i.e., 6 (six) out of 7 
(seven) Directors are Non-Executive Directors. GMDC is in the process of appointing 1 (one) more Independent Director in 
consonance with requirements of Government of Gujarat to comply with Regulation 17 of Listing Regulations.
  As a State Government Public Sector Undertaking (PSU), the Company benets from a unique synergy between commercial 
acumen and administrative excellence. The Government of Gujarat appoints senior members of the Indian Administrative Service 
(IAS) to the Board. These ofcers bring "wide-angle" professional experience and a deep understanding of the State’s 
developmental priorities, ensuring that the Company’s objectives remain harmonised with public interest and regional economic 
advancement.
  The proles of the Directors are available on our website and can be accessed at https://www.gmdcltd.com/disclosure-under-
regulation-46-sebi-lodr/.   ANNEXURE VIIEnabling Billion Dreams of Viksit Bharat

xi. Information supplied to the Board
The Board meets at regular intervals to discuss and decide on business strategies/policies and review the nancial performance of the 
Company. The detailed agenda along with the relevant notes and other material information, are sent in advance, at least seven days before 
the Meeting, individually to each Director except for the meetings which are convened at a shorter notice. Requisite information as specied 
in Part - A of Schedule II of Regulation 17(7) of the Listing Regulations are made available to the Board of Directors, whenever applicable, for 
discussions and consideration at the Meeting. The Board has complete access to any information within the Company. 
At every Board Meeting, comprehensive presentations are made covering key areas such as nance, marketing, operations, project 
planning, policy matters and other material or signicant developments.
In cases of business exigencies or urgent matters, resolutions are passed by circulation. Such resolutions are subsequently placed before 
the Board or the respective Committee at the next meeting for noting and conrmation.
Signicant decisions taken at Board and Committee Meetings are systematically tracked until their closure. An Action Taken Report (ATR) on 
these decisions is presented at each meeting for the Board’s review. Additionally, the ATR pertaining to decisions from the previous Board 
and Committee Meetings is placed before the immediately succeeding meetings for noting.
In compliance with the applicable provisions of the Act and the Listing Regulations, the Board has constituted the requisite mandatory 
Committees. Meetings of these Committees are convened as and when required. The minutes of all Committee Meetings are placed before 
the Board for its information and noting.
The Board periodically reviews the compliance reports pertaining to laws applicable to the Company along with the corrective steps taken to 
address instances of non-compliance, if any.
Periodic site visits to plant facilities are organised for the Managing Director with rst-hand exposure to the Company’s ground-level 
operations. Chairman has also visited some of the plant facilities during FY 2025-26.
xii. Board’s Procedure
Apart from the matters which are to be decided by the Board as per relevant statutes and rules, all major decisions involving large capital 
expenditure, mobilisation of resources, R & R, land acquisition, pricing policies, loans and investments, policy relating to all borrowings and 
personnel matters including Employees’ compensation etc., are decided by the Board. 
The Board’s oversight extends to critical strategic and regulatory milestones, including the approval of Mine Closure Plans under the Mines 
and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act 1957, the execution of Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs), the awarding of major 
contracts, and the formulation of marketing and sales strategies.

The Board has constituted following Statutory Committees as required under the Act and Listing Regulations:
i. Audit Committee.
ii. Nomination and Remuneration Committee.
iii. Stakeholders Relationship Committee.
iv. Risk Management Committee.

of the Company;
• To monitor and oversee implementation of the risk management policy, including evaluating the adequacy of risk management systems;
• To periodically review the risk management policy, including by considering the changing industry dynamics and evolving complexity;
• To keep the board of directors informed about the nature and content of its discussions, recommendations and actions to be taken;

of such committees, as per the framework laid down by the board of directors.

17. VIGIL MECHANISM / WHISTLE BLOWER POLICY
 The Company has a Vigil Mechanism/Whistle Blower Policy for directors, employees, and other stakeholders to report genuine 
concerns regarding unethical behaviour, actual or suspected fraud, or violation of the Company's Code of Conduct. The Company 
being the Government Company is already covered under the government vigil mechanism. The Company ensures that strict 
condentially is maintained while dealing with the concerned. It also ensures that no discrimination is met out to any person for genially 
raised concern. The Vigil Mechanism is administered through the HR Department of the company under the guidance and supervision 
of Audit Committee. The Policy also has a provision of protection against victimisation against Whistle Blower and the Policy also 
provides for direct access to the Chairperson of the Audit Committee, in cases of exceptional / sensitive nature. The Policy is available 
on the website of the Company, https://www.gmdcltd.com/about/corporate-policies-gmdc/.

the Directors and the Management of the Company, we certify that the Company has complied with the conditions of Corporate 
Governance as stipulated in the SEBI Listing Regulations, 2015 except for the following:
i. As per Regulation 17(1)(b) of the SEBI Listing Regulations, where the regular Non-Executive Chairperson of the listed entity is a promoter of 
the listed entity or is related to any promoter, at least half of the Board of Directors shall comprise Independent Directors. The Chairperson of 
the Company is a Non-Executive Promoter Director (a nominee of the Government of Gujarat, being the promoter of the Company); 
accordingly, at least one-half of the Board of Directors is required to comprise Independent Directors. As on March 31, 2026, the Board 
comprises 7 (seven) Directors, of whom 3 (three) are Independent Directors, i.e. less than one-half, the shortfall having arisen with effect from 
January 22, 2026.
However, in this regard it has been informed to us by the management that Directors are appointed by the Government of Gujarat through its 
Administrative Ministry and regular representations have been made to the Administrative Ministry for appointment of Independent 
Director(s).
We state that as at March 31, 2026, no investor grievance was pending for a period of one month against the Company as per the records 
maintained by the Company and presented to the Stakeholders Relationship Committee.
