MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS REPORT ANNEXURE VIII
Economic Overview
FY 2025-26 reinforced the strategic importance of resource security, energy reliability and resilient domestic mineral supply chains. The 
global economy expanded at a measured pace as ination moderated and monetary conditions gradually stabilised. At the same time, 
geopolitical developments, evolving trade relationships and supply-chain diversication continued to elevate the strategic importance of 
minerals, energy resources and processing capabilities.
For mining and energy companies, competitive differentiation increasingly depended on supply reliability, logistics efciency, customer 
proximity and disciplined capital allocation. Demand drivers also became more diversied, supported by infrastructure development, 
manufacturing expansion, energy transition investments and technology-led applications.
India remained among the fastest-growing major economies during the year. Real GDP is estimated to have grown by 7.7%, while nominal 
GDP grew by 8.9%. Real GVA expanded by 7.9%, supported by robust growth in the secondary and tertiary sectors, which grew by 8.8% and 
9.3%, respectively. Private consumption and gross xed capital formation both remained above 7.5%, indicating resilient domestic demand 
and continued investment momentum across key sectors of the economy.
Against this backdrop, GMDC is well positioned to benet from the strengthening linkage between economic growth, industrial 
development and mineral demand. As infrastructure, manufacturing and strategic mineral initiatives continue to scale, demand visibility is 
widening across the Company’s resource portfolio, including lignite, bauxite, manganese, silica sand, limestone and emerging mineral 
opportunities. This gives a p latform to enhance resource monetisation through reliable supply, customer-focussed market development, 
quality assurance, beneciation and value-added offerings.
The broader operating environment is increasingly inuencing project development, market access, energy security, critical mineral 
capability and capital deployment decisions. Accordingly, the following sections analyse the global and domestic environment and their 
implications for the Company’s business performance, growth initiatives and strategic priorities.
Global Economic Environment
The global economy entered FY 2025-26 with moderate but resilient growth momentum. While economic performance varied across 
regions, overall growth remained positive. The IMF projects global growth at 3.1% in 2026 and 3.2% in 2027, indicating a stable growth 
environment than broad-based cyclical expansion. Ination continued to ease from prior peaks but remained sensitive to energy prices, 
logistics costs and geopolitical developments.

Mining and Mineral Sector Outlook
India’s mining sector is entering a more execution-focussed phase, characterised by faster project development, deeper exploration, 
commercial mining expansion, critical mineral development and improved logistics integration. The policy framework increasingly favours 
mining enterprises that can combine geological expertise, project governance, technology adoption, stakeholder management and market 
access to convert resources into commercially viable operations.
During the year, policy initiatives shifted from broad reform objectives to implementation-led measures. Regulatory emphasis centred on 
accelerating approvals, digitising exploration processes, integrating mine closure planning, expanding commercial mining and 
strengthening critical mineral development. As a result, the operating environment has become more conducive to project execution, with 
greater attention on statutory-readiness, technical validation and time-bound development milestones.
A notable development was the launch of the SWCS Exploration Module in July 2025, which digitised the submission, review and approval of 
geological reports. This was complemented by the notication of 18 additional QCI-NABET accredited prospecting agencies for coal and 
lignite exploration in November 2025, a measure expected to reduce prospecting licence timelines by nearly six months. Collectively, these 
initiatives enhance transparency, improve work-ow efciency and strengthen project sequencing.
The regulatory framework for mine planning also underwent a signicant change. Under the revised guidelines issued by the Ministry of 
Coal, the Mine Closure Plan now forms an integral part of the Mining Plan, eliminating the requirement for separate approval. This integrated 
approach embeds environmental management, land restoration, safety considerations, and community commitments into project design, 
reinforcing responsible mining as a key determinant of project viability. 
For GMDC, these reforms have direct implications for project execution and capital allocation. Progress across new lignite mines in Gujarat, 
Odisha coal blocks, copper development, limestone partnerships and critical mineral initiatives will increasingly depend on approval 
efciency, technical preparedness and integrated project planning. This evolving framework also strengthens investor condence by 
promoting greater visibility on project timelines, environmental obligations and long-term sustainability outcomes.
Commercial mining expanded further during the year. Captive and commercial coal production reached 210.46 MT as of 31 March 2026, 
reecting growth of 10.22%, while despatch increased by 7.35% to 204.61 MT. The operationalisation of 12 additional coal blocks added 
more than 86 MT of annual production capacity, highlighting the growing scale and competitiveness of the sector. This reinforces the 
importance of efcient mine planning, logistics capability, cost visibility and customer development.
Critical minerals emerged as a major policy priority. In September 2025, the Government launched the sixth tranche of critical mineral block 
auctions comprising 23 blocks across 13 States and Union Territories, spanning minerals such as rare earth elements, lithium, tungsten, 
niobium, graphite, titanium and vanadium. Together with previous auction rounds, this reects a sustained national effort to build secure and 
diversied mineral supply chains. Production and Despatch figures in MT

The sector is also moving towards real-time visibility, automated workows and data-led operating control. IoT-enabled eet monitoring,

relevant because they link technology directly to mine-to-market outcomes, including equipment use, vehicle cycles, despatch visibility, 
grade communication and coordination across operating teams.
Beneciation and value addition are becoming central to mineral competitiveness. In bauxite, silica sand, uorspar, copper and rare earths, 
future value is likely to come not only from mine output, but from grade consistency, blending capability, processing depth, downstream 
linkages and customer-specic applications. The sector is therefore moving from bulk despatch towards t-for-purpose mineral solutions.
These trends align closely with the next phase of the Company’s project pipeline. New lignite mines in Gujarat, Odisha coal blocks, the 
Ambaji Copper Project, limestone-linked partnerships, rare earth initiatives and mineral intelligence platforms all depend on faster 
approvals, mine closure integration, technical-readiness, digital operating systems and market linkage. The implication for the Company is 
that Lakshya 2030 needs to be read not only as a growth aspiration, but as a project-conversion agenda: moving from resources to 
permitted projects, from mineral output to customer-specic products, and from conventional mining to a more technology-enabled 
minerals platform.
Energy Sector Outlook
India’s energy sector in FY 2025-26 reected a pragmatic transition, where renewable energy, coal and lignite each carried a distinct role in 
meeting power and industrial needs. The outlook remains balanced, with renewable capacity expanding rapidly while domestic solid fuels 
retain relevance for base-load power, industrial energy security and grid reliability.
India achieved the 1 billion tonne coal production milestone for the second consecutive year on 20 March 2026, reecting the strategic place 
of domestic coal in the national energy system. This milestone shows that energy transition in India is progressing alongside fuel-security 
priorities, rather than replacing them in the near term.
Fuel access frameworks are moving towards greater exibility, with policy measures such as Revised SHAKTI giving power generators more 
options to align coal linkages with market requirements. This supports wider use of domestic coal while improving responsiveness across 
the power sector.
The policy environment also created new momentum for coal and lignite gasication. In May 2026, the Union Cabinet approved a surface 
coal and lignite gasication scheme with an outlay of H37,500 crore. The scheme targets gasication of about 75 MT of coal and lignite coal 
and lignite, and provides incentives up to 20% of plant and machinery cost, and extends coal linkage tenure for syngas projects up to 30 
years. This opens a technology-led route for solid fuel resources across syngas, methanol, hydrogen and industrial fuel substitution, subject 
to technical-readiness, feedstock suitability, offtake arrangements and commercial viability.
Lignite operations showed stronger momentum toward the close of FY 2025-26, with production increasing by 12% in the quarter ended 
March 2026. The Company also focussed on supply preparedness through planned lignite production of over 20 lakh MT for the monsoon 
period, supported by covered stockpiles, 24x7 mechanised quality monitoring across mines, an upgraded customer booking portal and a 
volume-based discount scheme at Bhavnagar Mine.
Coastal lignite movement added a new route to market. During the year, sea-route despatch coordinated through EOI customers reached 
approximately 39,000 MT, including around 31,000 MT in March 2026. The rst movement from Bhavnagar port to Karanja port in 
Maharashtra marked the start of interstate lignite movement by sea, providing a practical template for serving customers beyond 
conventional road-linked catchments.
Over the next three to ve years, India’s energy sector is expected to require both renewable capacity addition and dependable 
despatchable power. This creates a balanced role for GMDC across lignite, coal, LTPS, renewables and gasication-linked options. Energy 
security and energy transition are therefore not separate narratives for the Company. Mine-readiness, logistics exibility, plant reliability, 
reclaimed land-based renewables and cleaner fuel pathways together dene how the energy business is positioned to serve Gujarat’s 
industrial needs while aligning with India’s resource and transition priorities.
Product-wise External Environment
Coal and Lignite Sector Perspective
Production and Growth Overview
India’s coal and lignite sector in FY 2025-26 moved further into a reliability-led phase. Domestic coal availability became a central support for 
power generation, industrial fuel security and import substitution. 
Commercial and captive mining also gained wider relevance. As on 31 March 2026, production from captive and commercial coal mines 
reached 210.46 MT, growing by 10.22% over the previous year, while despatch stood at 204.61 MT, growing by 7.35%. During the year, 12 
blocks were operationalised, adding more than 86 MT of annual production capacity. This shift is changing the coal market from a largely 
allocation-led model to a more diversied production ecosystem. 
For GMDC, coal and lignite are not only fuel sources. They are instruments of energy reliability, customer assurance and regional industrial 
competitiveness. As the Company takes forward Odisha coal blocks and new lignite projects in Gujarat, value creation is dependent on 
project-readiness, clearances, land availability, logistics planning and market linkage.
Electricity Generation and Capacity Mix
India’s electricity system in FY 2025-26 showed a practical balance between scale and transition. Total electricity generation, including 
renewable energy, reached 1,845.921 BU, compared with 1,828.877 BU in the previous year, recording growth of 0.93%. Fossil fuel 
generation accounted for 1,306.951 BU, while non-fossil generation accounted for 538.97 BU, representing 29.2% of total generation. Coal-
based generation stood at 1,250.189 BU, showing that coal remains central to grid reliability even as renewable generation rises.

Government Policy Landscape
Exploration and Approval Reforms
Exploration activity during the year moved closer to project-readiness, with greater emphasis on digital workows, clearer approval tracking 
and stronger alignment between geological assessment and mine development. This shift supports a more structured approach to 
resource validation, statutory planning and future project conversion. The notication of 18 additional QCI-NABET accredited prospecting 
agencies widened technical capacity for coal and lignite exploration and is expected to shorten prospecting-related timelines.
Faster geological validation and online workows are supporting better project sequencing, particularly for mines that require coordination 
across technical, statutory and environmental workstreams. These measures are relevant to the Company’s new lignite mines, Odisha coal 
blocks and future mineral projects. Digital approvals and wider exploration capacity can support faster geological validation, better project 
planning and clearer investor visibility.
Revised SHAKTI Policy
SHAKTI, or the Scheme for Harnessing and Allocating Koyala Transparently in India, is the policy framework for transparent allocation of coal 
linkages to the power sector. The Revised SHAKTI Policy, approved in May 2025, simplied coal linkage allocation into two windows. 
Window I provides coal linkage to Central and State Gencos at notied price, while Window II allows generators to secure coal at a premium 
above notied price for periods up to 25 years. 
The removal of the power purchase agreement requirement under Window II gives generators greater exibility to align fuel procurement 
with market opportunities. This makes the policy relevant not only for fuel availability, but also for power-market responsiveness, plant 
economics and domestic coal offtake. For GMDC, the policy reinforces the need to view fuel supply and power generation as linked 
businesses, with lignite mining, LTPS operations and future energy projects assessed in relation to market requirements, fuel economics, 
despatch exibility and grid needs.
Coal Logistics Plan and Policy
The Coal Logistics Plan and Policy, launched in February 2024, stayed relevant through FY 2025-26 as implementation progressed across 
rst-mile connectivity, rail-based evacuation and multimodal movement. The plan aims to reduce rail logistics cost by 14% and generate 
annual savings of around H21,000 crore through a shift towards rail-based rst-mile connectivity systems. 
Implementation updates also show progress on rst-mile and multimodal systems. As per Ministry disclosures, 39 rst-mile connectivity 
projects with capacity of 386 MT had been completed, and coal movement through the Rail-Sea-Rail route rose from around 28 MT in FY 
2021-22 to around 54 MT in FY 2023-24. 
Coal logistics is gradually moving towards integrated and multimodal evacuation. Cost, reliability, volume commitment and route exibility 
are expected to become important factors in market access, particularly for customers located beyond traditional supply catchments. For 
the Company, the direction of national logistics is relevant to coastal lignite movement from Bhavnagar. As volumes are assessed, 
multimodal logistics can become a useful lever for customer access, landed-cost optimisation and market expansion.
Digital Coal Trading Exchange
Coal market reform also advanced through the proposed coal exchange framework. The Ministry of Coal moved the reform from concept to 
draft-rule stage, with the Coal Controller Organisation envisaged as the regulator and coal exchanges proposed as electronic platforms for 
transparent trading of coal and lignite. The December 2025 draft rules indicated a shift towards a structured market with improved price 
discovery and wider participation by sellers and buyers. The Coal Controller Organisation has also created a dedicated Coal Exchange 
portal as a public window for policy visibility, document access, notices and application-readiness. 
As coal and lignite trading becomes more transparent, commercial decisions are expected to depend more on grade assurance, supply 
reliability, despatch responsiveness and market intelligence. This creates relevance beyond pricing alone. A more visible trading 
environment places greater importance on quality communication, customer segmentation, faster contracting and data-led sales 
decisions, particularly as the Company widens customer access across existing and potential markets.
Mining Plan and Mine Closure Guidelines
The Ministry of Coal issued the Guidelines for Preparation of Mining Plan and Mine Closure Plan for Coal and Lignite Mines, 2025 on 31 
January 2025. The guidelines make the Mine Closure Plan, including the Final Mine Closure Plan, an integral part of the Mining Plan. 
This brings closure planning into the project design stage. Mine planning now has to account not only for extraction sequencing, but also 
restoration, safety, land use, community obligations and end-of-life accountability. For mining companies, this creates a m ore integrated 
planning approach, where technical viability, environmental safeguards and local acceptance are assessed together from the beginning.
The framework is relevant to the next phase of lignite, coal and future mineral projects. As the Company moves new projects through 
approvals, land-readiness, environmental planning and site development, early integration of closure planning is expected to support 
smoother project movement and responsible long-duration mining operations.Enabling Billion Dreams of Viksit Bharat

Coal Gasication and Syngas Schemes
Coal and lignite gasication gained policy focus as a long-term route to convert solid fuel resources into syngas and downstream industrial 
fuels, subject to technology-readiness, feedstock suitability, offtake and commercial viability. This opens a technology-led route for solid fuel 
resources, with possible applications across syngas, methanol, hydrogen and industrial fuel substitution. At the same time, the business 
case for gasication is likely to depend on feedstock quality, capital cost, technology-readiness, environmental performance and offtake 
arrangements. The opportunity is relevant because the Company has coal and lignite resources in Gujarat and Odisha, and such resources 
may nd wider applications if technology, partners and downstream economics align. This positions gasication as a selective long-term 
option within the Company’s broader energy security narrative.
Performance of GMDC: Lignite
GMDC’s lignite business in FY 2025-26 reected the practical value of local fuel security. The Company achieved lignite despatch of 78.84 
lakh MT against a target of 81.40 lakh MT, despite early and extended monsoon conditions, severe waterlogging at Tadkeshwar and 
demand impact in the Morbi industrial cluster due to gas supply constraints. Lignite revenue stood at approximately H2,339 crore.
The fourth quarter showed the operating depth of the business. GMDC recorded quarterly lignite despatch of 25.82 lakh MT, the highest 
quarterly despatch in the last seven years. Bhavnagar Mine emerged as a key supply centre, achieving its highest-ever annual despatch of 
25.47 lakh MT against a target of 25.40 lakh MT. It also recorded its highest-ever monthly despatch of 3.63 lakh MT and has an estimated 
balance mine life of around 15 years.
Coastal movement of lignite added a new dimension to market reach. During the year, lignite movement through coastal shipping 
coordinated through EOI customers reached around 39,000 MT, including around 31,000 MT in March 2026. The rst interstate movement 
from Bhavnagar port to Karanja port in Maharashtra created a practical template for reaching customers beyond Gujarat through sea 
logistics.
The year also sharpened the operating priorities for FY 2026-27. GMDC’s lignite despatch target of 97 lakh MT will depend on lignite 
exposure, monsoon preparedness, quality consistency, faster truck turnaround, customer engagement and market conditions. The 
planned Urja-Setu initiative, online slot booking at Bhavnagar and quality optimisation at Mata-no-Madh can help convert mine-readiness 
into stronger customer offtake.
For GMDC, lignite is expected to be an important earnings contributor over the near and medium term. The focus will be on converting mine 
output into reliable customer supply through mine-readiness, exible logistics, customer support and consistent quality systems.

Outlook
The coal and lignite sector continues to play an important role in meeting growing electricity demand and supporting energy security, 
particularly in emerging economies. Supported by strong domestic demand and industrial activity, coal consumption and production are

expectations may influence long-term demand trends, coal and lignite are expected to remain key sources of baseload power and 
support industrial growth during the transition to a lower carbon energy mix.

Business and Product Performance
Minerals and Metals
Bauxite
India’s bauxite sector remains linked to aluminium demand, infrastructure activity and domestic raw-material security. Early FY 2025-26 data 
indicated positive momentum, with production rising from 1.87 MMT in April 2024 to 2.13 MMT in April 2025, a growth of 13.9%. The sector’s 
relevance is expected to increase as aluminium demand, cement applications, refractory uses and industrial self-reliance priorities support 
long-term raw-material demand. 
The Aluminium Vision Document released in 2025 provides a longer-term direction for the sector. It envisages scaling aluminium production 
sixfold by 2047 and expanding bauxite production capacity to 150 MTPA, along with higher recycling, low-carbon technologies and raw 
material security. This points to a market where bauxite value is expected to depend not only on availability, but also on grade consistency, 
blending capability, beneciation and supply suitability for end-use industries.
Within the non-lignite mineral business of the Company, bauxite is becoming a more active opportunity. A signicant portion of Minerals & 
Metals revenue was driven by the bauxite business, supported by auction-led market discovery and demand across cement, refractories, 
alumina-linked sectors and industrial applications. During the year, 4.13 lakh MT was sold through the Gadhsisa auction at a premium of 
around 63% over the base price, demonstrating the role of transparent price discovery, grade-led positioning and trusted supply quality.
The year’s outcome indicates that bauxite has moved beyond a volume-led opportunity. With the Minerals & Metals Division achieving 
despatches exceeding 30 lakh MT and revenue of approximately H179 crore, bauxite provides a practical base for building higher-yield 
mineral businesses outside lignite. The next stage is likely to be shaped by repeatable customer segments, auction design, grade 
consistency, customer-specic supply and beneciation potential, while retaining attention on permissions, logistics cost, customer 
concentration and demand cyclicality.
Silica Sand
Silica sand recorded one of the most notable growth outcomes within the Minerals & Metals Division. Revenue stood at approximately H36 
crore, while despatch growth exceeded 300% over the previous year, making it the fastest-growing mineral segment during the period. This 
performance builds on the sharp increase seen in FY 2025-26, when silica sand sales had reached 20.91 lakh MT, reecting a clear upward 
demand trajectory. This performance is particularly relevant because silica sand demand is becoming more specication-led, with 
customers placing higher value on purity, consistency and suitability for glass and solar-linked applications.
Demand for silica sand is increasingly linked to glass, ceramics, foundry, construction and solar glass applications. India’s solar capacity 
reached 157.05 GW as on 31 May 2026, creating a larger demand base for glass and related materials. 
The business gained relevance as demand from industrial and renewable-linked applications deepened. Its commercial pathway is likely to 
be shaped by impurity control, consistent quality, beneciation and reliable despatch rather than volume alone. For the Company, silica 
sand offers a credible route to develop a quality-led industrial mineral business with customer applications beyond conventional 
construction demand. For this business, beneciation and impurity control can become the difference between bulk mineral sales and entry 
into higher-value industrial applications.
Fluorspar
The uorspar business recorded a material recovery in commercial activity, with despatch and revenue growth exceeding 220% during the 
year. This marked an important step for a mineral that carries industrial relevance across chemicals, metallurgy and specialised 
applications. Fluorspar is not only a volume-led mineral. Its business potential depends on processing reliability, grade acceptance and 
access to specialised industrial customers. The recovery also reects operating stabilisation and renewed customer engagement after the 
earlier revamp of the Ambadungar Fluorspar Mine and Kadipani Beneciation Plant.
Beyond its revenue contribution, the project carries regional signicance. The mine and beneciation facility are located in an area with 
limited industrial presence, creating employment and local economic activity, particularly for nearby tribal communities. The project also 
gives GMDC an opportunity to link mineral development with local economic participation in a region where formal industrial activity is 
limited. The focus now is to convert the project’s revived operating base into consistent product quality, dependable supply and wider 
market acceptance.

Power and Energy
Akrimota Thermal Power Station (LTPS)
The power segment reported higher revenue during the year, with segment revenue rising to H215.72 crore from H160.28 crore in the 
previous year. At the same time, the segment recorded an operating loss of H79.61 crore, indicating that the turnaround of Akrimota Thermal 
Power Station is still in progress and central to the power business. The widening loss makes LTPS a management priority, where the quality 
of turnaround will be measured by plant availability, heat-rate performance, maintenance reliability and xed-cost absorption rather than 
generation alone.
The station has strategic relevance because it provides forward integration for lignite and supports regional power reliability. The year’s 
nancial performance points to the need for better plant availability, maintenance planning, heat-rate performance, fuel logistics and xed-
cost absorption. The proposed exploration of a 350 MW lignite-based thermal expansion at LTPS also places the asset within a b roader 
energy-security context, subject to technical, regulatory and commercial evaluation.
The business priority is therefore not only higher generation, but a more predictable operating model. A nancially healthier LTPS can 
support lignite value capture, provide despatchable power capacity and contribute to Gujarat’s industrial energy ecosystem.
Renewable Energy
The renewable energy business provides a measured complement to the Company’s mining and thermal energy activities. The asset base 
comprises 201 and 5 MW of installed renewable capacity, including wind and solar projects, with generation of ~327 and 6.5 MU 
respectively reported for the period. The renewable base also gives GMDC an operating reference point for balancing mining-led cash ows 
with lower-carbon generation assets.
India’s renewable energy capacity, excluding large hydro, stood at 230.78 GW as on 31 March 2026, with solar and wind capacity forming 
the largest parts of this base. This national energy mix creates mineral demand for solar glass, aluminium, copper, rare earth magnets and 
transmission infrastructure, linking GMDC’s mineral direction with India’s energy transition priorities.
The segment also supports the Company’s transition-readiness narrative. The opportunity ahead lies in evaluating renewable projects 
where site availability, evacuation infrastructure, commercial offtake and mining-linked land assets create a viable case. This approach 
allows the energy business to connect resource development with long-term land productivity and transition-linked energy needs.
Wind
Wind energy is the larger component of the renewable energy business, with 201 MW across 7 wind projects. The projects provide recurring 
generation from a m ature asset base and add diversity to the Company’s earnings prole. The maturity of these assets makes machine 
availability, preventive maintenance and site-level generation planning more important than capacity addition alone. In the context of India’s 
rising renewable capacity, these assets also support a balanced energy mix.
The operating focus for wind assets is centred on machine availability, generation efciency, site-level maintenance and cost control. With 
renewable generation becoming more competitive and grid-linked, asset performance will depend on technical upkeep, scheduling 
discipline and timely interventions across high-generation sites. In a m ore competitive renewable market, performance gains are likely to 
come from asset productivity, not only tariff or capacity.
Solar
The solar business is anchored by the Panandhro solar plant, with installed capacity of 5 MW, developed on reclaimed mine land. The 
project has signicance beyond generation because it demonstrates productive reuse of mined land and links mining operations with 
renewable energy creation.

grade communication. Modern analytical tools, digital workows and site-level monitoring are likely to aid despatch decisions, improve Enabling Billion Dreams of Viksit Bharat

Exploration Activities – From Resource Assessment to Project-Readiness
Exploration activity during FY 2025-26 was directed towards converting mineral potential into development-readiness. The focus extended 
beyond identifying resources to building the technical base required for mine planning, beneciation, statutory approvals and market-linked 
mineral development. This marks an important shift in the role of exploration, where geological assessment is increasingly tied to bankable 
projects, specication-led products and revenue pathways.
At Ambaji, the copper project was a key exploration and development priority. The project is positioned as Gujarat’s rst underground 
copper mine and carries signicance for India’s copper, zinc and lead value chain. During the year, the mining plan and mine closure plan 
for the Ambaji Copper Project were handed over by IBM, marking movement from geological assessment towards project structuring. The 
project has approximately 10 MT of copper, zinc and lead resources, planned beneciation capacity of 500 KTPA and a projected mine life 
of more than 21 years.
Lignite exploration and reserve conversion also carried signicance during the year. With legacy mines at different stages of maturity, future 
supply is linked to timely development of new lignite blocks across Kutch and South Gujarat. Exploration in blocks such as Bharkandam, 
EFG Valia and Ghala assists reserve conversion, mine design and project economics, while giving the Company a clearer basis to plan fuel 
availability for Gujarat industrial customers.
The direction ahead is to connect exploration more closely with bankability and market t. Geological work is likely to be assessed alongside 
mine closure planning, logistics, grade parameters, beneciation routes and customer demand. This approach moves exploration from a 
resource-identication activity to a foundation for responsible mining, application-led supply and long-term business growth.
New Frontiers – FY 2025-26 Priorities Across Energy, Minerals and Future Resources
FY 2025-26 gave clearer shape to the next phase across coal, lignite, copper, rare earths, limestone and gasication-linked options. The 
direction is not diversication for its own sake. It reects a measured move into minerals and energy assets connected with industrial growth, 
fuel security and strategic mineral priorities for India.
This shift also reects the wider role expected from a state mineral enterprise. GMDC is positioned to serve Gujarat industrial requirements, 
participate in resource security priorities for India and build businesses that combine reliable supply, processing capability, customer 
access and responsible mining practices.
Each growth platform is being assessed through a dened business lens covering resource quality, approval-readiness, policy t, customer 
use, environmental safeguards and commercial viability. This creates a practical basis for capital allocation across near-term earnings 
contributors and longer-gestation mineral and energy assets.
Ambaji Copper Project – Moving Towards Project Structuring
The Ambaji Copper Project places the Company in a mineral that is central to transmission networks, renewable energy, electric mobility, 
industrial electronics and manufacturing. Copper also has direct relevance to India’s energy transition, making the project important beyond 
its regional mining footprint.
The project comprises approximately 10 MT of copper, zinc and lead resources, with planned beneciation capacity of 500 KTPA and a 
projected mine life of more than 21 years. The handover of the mining plan and mine closure plan during FY 2025-26 added project clarity 
and created a base for technical, statutory and investment-related decisions.
The project pathway depends on more than ore extraction. Beneciation performance, metallurgical recovery, underground mining 
capability, environmental safeguards and market linkage for multiple metal streams are likely to dene its commercial outcome. Ambaji 
therefore represents entry into a more complex mineral category, where technical depth and phased project movement carry as much 
weight as resource size.
Odisha Coal Blocks – Building the Next Energy Resource Base
The Odisha coal blocks are central to the Company’s long-term energy resource plan. Baitarni West, Burapahar and Kudanali Lubri together 
give access to large coal resources outside Gujarat and create an opportunity to serve wider industrial and power-sector demand.
Baitarni West is the agship block, with more than 1,000 MT of geological reserves and peak capacity of 15 MTPA. Across the three Odisha 
coal blocks, the resource base exceeds 2 billion tonnes, giving the Company a substantial future coal platform. The FY 2024-25 Integrated 
Annual Report had positioned these assets as part of the long-term growth plan, with Baitarni West targeted for operations by FY 2026.
During FY 2025-26, the focus was on moving the blocks through the project-readiness chain: land, clearances, rehabilitation, mining 
contracts, evacuation and customer linkage. These blocks provide long-term earnings potential, with value creation linked to the conversion 
of geological reserves into permitted, evacuated and market-linked production.
New Lignite Mines – Preparing Gujarat’s Future Industrial Fuel Supply
New lignite mines are critical to industrial fuel security in Gujarat. As existing mines mature, the next phase of supply is linked to timely 
development of new blocks across Kutch and South Gujarat.
The lignite pipeline includes Lakhpat Punhrajpur, Damlai, EFG Valia, Panandhro Extension, Bharkandam and Ghala. Together, these mines 
are expected to add a large reserve base for long-term supply to industrial users in Gujarat.

Limestone and Cement Sector Integration – Converting Mineral Access into Industrial Partnerships
Limestone provides a route to connect mineral ownership with downstream industrial development. The limestone resources of GMDC in 
western Kutch are strategically located and provide scope to catalyse cement-led investment, regional employment and state revenue 
generation.
The Company has access to more than 2.5 billion tonnes of cement-grade limestone in western Kutch. Under the rst wave of limestone 
development, 800 MT was offered to cement players, and a 40-year limestone supply agreement was signed with J K Cement.
The opportunity goes beyond raw material supply. Limestone can help catalyse cement manufacturing in western Kutch, particularly when 
combined with lignite availability and port-linked logistics. This creates a long-duration raw material partnership model rather than a short-
cycle mineral sale model.
From an FY 2025-26 perspective, the priority is coordination across partner timelines, land-readiness, environmental approvals, water 
availability and infrastructure. The asset has long-term potential, with commercial movement linked to alignment across private investment, 
statutory processes and site development.
Rare Earths and Critical Minerals – Building India-linked Strategic Mineral Capability
Rare earths and critical minerals are becoming central to India’s industrial and technology agenda. Their role extends across electric 
mobility, renewable energy, electronics, defence systems and advanced manufacturing.
The rare earth initiative at Ambadungar and Bharuch places GMDC within this national priority. The FY 2024-25 Integrated Annual Report 
outlined more than 1 million tonnes of TREO, planned production of around 18,000 TPA of mixed rare earth carbonate, a 12,000 TPA TREO 
separation plant at Bharuch and around 1,800 TPA of Nd-Pr oxide capacity.
During FY 2025-26, this direction gained depth through partnerships and technology linkages. The Company entered into an MoU with 
NMDC for potential rare earth value chain development, received indigenous rare earth processing technology support from BARC for pilot-
scale validation, and partnered with the University of Cambridge to establish an AI-powered Rare Earth Supply Chain Observatory at iCEM. 
The rare earth pathway is likely to be phase-wise. These minerals require beneciation, separation, processing technology, environmental 
safeguards, market qualication and specialist capability. The opportunity is material, but technically demanding. A partnership-led 
approach helps manage learning risk while positioning GMDC within the critical mineral security agenda of India.
Coal Gasication – Evaluating Future Uses for Coal and Lignite
Coal and lignite gasication provide a technology-led route to widen the use of solid fuel resources. The opportunity lies in converting coal 
and lignite into syngas and downstream products such as methanol, hydrogen, fertiliser inputs and industrial fuels. The policy setting 
became more supportive, with the approved surface coal and lignite gasication scheme providing incentives and longer linkage tenure for 
syngas projects. The opportunity remains subject to technology-readiness, feedstock suitability, offtake and commercial viability.
GMDC has explored gasication opportunities through collaborations linked to coal and lignite resources in Gujarat and Odisha. 
Gasication is best viewed as a long-term option rather than an immediate earnings driver. The business case is likely to depend on 
technology-readiness, feedstock quality, capital cost, offtake arrangements, environmental performance and downstream product 
economics. Where these factors align, gasication may extend the role of coal and lignite in a changing energy landscape.
Renewable Energy – Linking Reclaimed Land, Clean Energy and Long-term Asset Use
Renewable energy forms a complementary part of the Company’s energy direction. The existing renewable base includes 205.9 MW of 
installed capacity across wind and solar projects, with generation of 327.52 MU reported for the period.
The solar project at Panandhro is signicant because it uses reclaimed mine land. This creates a practical link between land restoration and 
energy generation, showing how mined land can be redeployed for productive use after mining activity.
The renewable opportunity is likely to be shaped by site availability, grid connectivity, commercial offtake, hybrid models and mining-linked 
land assets. Rather than being viewed as a separate business line, renewables provide a route to connect land use, transition-readiness and 
long-term resource planning.
The direction ahead is to pursue renewable opportunities where they are commercially sound, operationally feasible and aligned with the 
asset base. This approach connects energy transition with mining rehabilitation, industrial customer needs and responsible long-term asset 
use.

Our Sustainability Pathway
The Company’s sustainability pathway is built around responsible mining, clean energy, resource efciency, community development, and 
strong governance. The Company has already taken several measures in this direction, including renewable energy generation through its 
205.9 MW wind and solar portfolio, Zero Liquid Discharge systems, water recycling, rainwater harvesting, green belt development, mine 
reclamation, biodiversity initiatives, and digital monitoring of operations. Its ESG agenda is guided by dened pillars covering responsible 
minerals, inclusive development, ethical governance, and a conscious value chain, supported by BRSR disclosures, ISO certications, 
materiality assessment, and regular performance reviews. 
Going forward, GMDC aims to deepen this sustainability pathway through clean energy transition initiatives, critical minerals development, 
coal and lignite gasication, blue hydrogen pilots, rare earth value chain development, digital mining, AI-enabled analytics, and improved 
resource productivity. The Company also plans to continue expanding its social impact through healthcare, education, skill development, 
local employment, MSME sourcing, and community-focussed programmes in mining-linked regions. These initiatives position GMDC to 
create long-term value while supporting India’s energy security, industrial self-reliance, environmental responsibility, and inclusive regional 
growth.
2030 Growth Pathway and Strategic Priorities
The Company’s 2030 growth pathway – Lakshya 2030 – is built around four connected pillars. The rst is the existing lignite business, which 
provides the earnings base, customer reach and regional fuel relevance for Gujarat industrial users. The second is the expansion of the 
energy resource base through Odisha coal blocks, which adds a wider geographic platform and longer-duration resource visibility. The third 
is the move into strategic and transition-linked minerals, including copper, rare earth elements and limestone, which connect the business 
with resource security priorities for India, infrastructure growth, clean energy technologies and advanced manufacturing. The fourth is the 
use of partnerships, technology and processing capability to move into complex mineral value chains with a phased and commercially 
measured approach.
These pillars reect a business growth plan that is broader than capacity addition alone. The emphasis is on converting resource access into 
permitted, evacuated, quality-assured and customer-linked businesses. In lignite, this means mine-readiness, supply assurance, quality 
consistency and customer-linked despatch planning. In coal, it means land-readiness, statutory approvals, rehabilitation, mining 
arrangements, evacuation infrastructure and market linkage. In minerals such as copper, rare earths, limestone and bauxite, it means 
technical validation, beneciation potential, end-use suitability, environmental safeguards and customer qualication.
The growth plan also emphasises the changing nature of mineral demand. Industrial expansion in India requires dependable domestic fuel 
and bulk minerals, while energy transition and manufacturing priorities are increasing the role of copper, rare earths, silica sand, bauxite and 
other critical inputs. This places GMDC in a position where existing businesses provide near-term nancial resilience, while new mineral and 
energy opportunities offer a longer development runway.
Partnerships and technology are likely to play an important role in this transition. Complex areas such as rare earth processing, coal and 
lignite gasication, mineral intelligence and new energy pathways require specialist capability, technical validation and market alignment. A 
partnership-led model provides scope to manage learning curves, access domain expertise and assess viability before larger capital 
deployment.
Lakshya 2030 is not a separate strategic statement; it is the connecting logic across lignite, coal, copper, rare earths, limestone, renewables 
and gasication-linked opportunities. The pathway points to a m ore integrated minerals and energy enterprise, where growth is linked to 
supply reliability, project conversion, customer-specic mineral solutions, responsible mining and careful capital phasing aligned with 
Gujarat industrial requirements and resource security priorities for India.
Responsible Mining and Resource Stewardship
For over six decades, GMDC has played a vital role in developing Gujarat’s mineral resources while supporting regional economic growth. 
As a State-owned enterprise, the Company views mining as a long-term responsibility – one that balances resource development with 
environmental stewardship, employee safety and community well-being.
GMDC’s approach to responsible mining extends across the entire asset lifecycle, from exploration and mine planning to operations, 
reclamation and post-mining land use. Sustainability considerations are increasingly integrated into project evaluation and development, 
ensuring that environmental, social and safety factors are addressed alongside operational and economic objectives.
The Company continues to focus on scientic mining practices, efcient resource utilisation and progressive land restoration. Environmental 
management measures covering land rehabilitation, water conservation, emission control and ecological restoration form an integral part of 
operational discipline. Initiatives such as Napier grass plantation and other reclamation measures support the rehabilitation of disturbed 
land and promote long-term environmental value creation.
GMDC’s commitment to resource stewardship is also reected in its efforts to create productive outcomes from operating assets and by-
products. The Panandhro solar project on reclaimed mining land demonstrates how former mine areas can be repurposed to support clean 
energy generation. Similarly, the utilisation of y ash in mine restoration and y ash brick applications contributes to circular resource use and 
environmental improvement.

Data-led Operations and Intelligent Systems
Technology is becoming an increasingly important enabler of GMDC’s growth and operational efciency. As the Company expands across

experience and support faster decision-making across the mine-to-market value chain.
GMDC’s digital transformation is guided by a business-led approach focussed on improving operational excellence, responsiveness and 
stakeholder engagement. Customer-facing platforms already enable services such as online despatch order booking, customer 
registration, coal distribution management and digital support systems, promoting greater transparency and ease of access.
The Company’s technology investments are increasingly directed towards measurable business outcomes. Fleet monitoring, weighbridge

nance and customer-facing functions. These initiatives support greater operational discipline while enabling faster and more informed 
decision-making across GMDC’s geographically dispersed operations.
The next phase of transformation is expected to be driven by data, analytics and intelligent technologies. In the mining sector, articial 
intelligence and advanced analytics have growing relevance in areas such as demand forecasting, eet productivity, grade modelling,

Alongside digital adoption, the Company continues to focus on strengthening operational controls and system resilience. As business 
processes become more technology-enabled, areas such as cybersecurity, system availability, access management, data quality and 
governance assume greater importance. Robust digital controls support both business continuity and stakeholder condence, particularly 
across customer platforms, despatch systems, ERP-based processes and project monitoring frameworks.
Looking ahead, GMDC’s digital vision is centred on integrating mine operations, quality assurance, sales planning, procurement, nance, 
safety and project execution into a unied decision-making environment. By combining technology, analytics and business processes, the 
Company aims to convert operational data into actionable insights, enhance organisational agility and build a future-ready platform for 
sustainable growth.
Navigating Risks, Unlocking Opportunities
The operating environment during FY 2025-26 underscored the importance of balancing growth ambitions with operational resilience. 
Market dynamics, mine availability, climatic conditions, regulatory processes and changing customer requirements continued to inuence 
business performance. At the same time, opportunities emerged through domestic resource development, expansion of strategic mineral 
capabilities, progress in coal and copper initiatives, and growing interest in critical minerals that support India's long-term resource security.
GMDC's enterprise risk management framework is embedded within planning and decision-making processes. The Company actively 
monitors risks relating to mining operations, project execution, resource availability, market competition, regulatory compliance, 
environmental management, safety performance, IT systems and infrastructure reliability. This integrated approach enables timely risk 
mitigation while supporting sustainable growth and operational continuity.
Looking ahead, the Company's ability to advance new projects, diversify its resource portfolio and strengthen operating efciency will remain 
key drivers of long-term value creation. By combining disciplined risk management with strategic investment priorities, GMDC aims to 
enhance resilience and capitalise on emerging opportunities across the mining and energy value chain.
Risks 
As GMDC expands its portfolio across lignite, coal, limestone, copper, rare earth elements and other strategic minerals, effective project 
execution remains critical to unlocking long-term value. The development of new projects depends on timely land acquisition, statutory and 
environmental approvals, infrastructure creation, rehabilitation planning and stakeholder coordination. Delays in these areas can affect 
project timelines and capital deployment; accordingly, the Company continues to monitor approval-related risks closely through focussed 
project-level interventions and governance mechanisms.
Operational continuity remains another important business priority. During FY 2025-26, extended monsoon conditions and waterlogging at 
certain mining locations impacted production and despatch activities. In response, GMDC continues to strengthen mine planning, pit 
preparedness, drainage systems, dewatering arrangements, stockpile management, quality control and logistics-readiness to improve 
operational resilience and maintain supply reliability.
Market dynamics also continue to inuence business performance. Changes in fuel economics, competition from imported materials and 
supply disruptions affecting customer industries can impact demand patterns. To address these challenges, the Company is focussed on Enabling Billion Dreams of Viksit Bharat

strengthening customer engagement, improving market intelligence, enhancing logistics exibility and adopting a more data-driven 
approach to customer segmentation and market development.
Product quality remains a key differentiator in maintaining customer condence and supporting commercial competitiveness. The 
Company's NABL-accredited laboratories at Bhavnagar and Mata-no-Madh strengthen testing capabilities and quality assurance 
processes. As GMDC expands its presence across minerals such as bauxite, silica sand, uorspar and future strategic resources, 
laboratory reliability, sampling accuracy, grade communication and traceability will become increasingly important in supporting customer 
requirements and value realisation.
In the power business, plant efciency, availability and cost optimisation remain important performance drivers. Continuous monitoring, 
preventive maintenance and adherence to overhaul schedules are aimed at improving operational performance at the Akrimota Thermal 
Power Station (LTPS). Reliable plant operations not only support business performance but also strengthen the integration between mining 
and power generation activities.
Technology resilience is becoming increasingly important as operations become more digitally integrated. The Company continues to 
enhance system reliability through cloud-based infrastructure, backup systems, disaster recovery measures and ERP-driven process 
improvements. As digital platforms become central to customer engagement, quality monitoring, logistics and business decision-making, 
maintaining system availability, data integrity and cybersecurity remains a key focus area.
Environmental, safety and social considerations are closely integrated into GMDC's growth strategy. As the Company progresses new 
projects within and beyond Gujarat, emphasis is being placed on regulatory compliance, water management, rehabilitation planning, 
biodiversity conservation, workforce safety, community engagement and mine closure planning. These factors are increasingly important in 
securing approvals, maintaining stakeholder trust and supporting long-term asset sustainability.
In addition, procurement efciency, contractor performance, equipment reliability and maintenance planning remain critical to operational 
success. Strong vendor management practices, preventive maintenance programmes and infrastructure-readiness help support 
production continuity, project execution, despatch reliability and customer service. As project activity expands, these capabilities will play an 
increasingly important role in delivering operational excellence and sustainable growth.
Opportunities
GMDC’s growth opportunities are increasingly anchored in its ability to convert a diversied mineral portfolio into sustainable commercial 
value. While lignite continues to be the Company’s principal business, evolving customer requirements, logistics innovation and emerging 
opportunities in strategic minerals are creating multiple avenues for future growth.
A key opportunity lies in strengthening the reliability of mine-to-customer supply. Demand from industrial clusters across Gujarat continues 
to underline the importance of dependable domestic fuel sources, particularly during periods of volatility in imported fuels and alternative 
energy markets. Accordingly, the Company remains focussed on enhancing mine-readiness, quality consistency, logistics efciency and 
customer servicing capabilities to support stable supply and improve market responsiveness.
The Company is also placing greater emphasis on customer-centric growth. Through customer mapping, direct industry engagement, 
digital sales platforms and initiatives such as the proposed Urja-Setu boiler advisory programme, GMDC is deepening its understanding of 
fuel consumption patterns and customer requirements. These efforts are expected to support stronger customer retention, improved market 
penetration and more targeted commercial strategies across industrial segments.
Logistics remains an important growth enabler. The successful experience of coastal lignite movement has highlighted the potential to 
expand market reach beyond traditional road-based supply networks. By improving access to distant customer markets and enhancing 
evacuation exibility, multimodal logistics solutions can support higher market penetration while improving supply chain resilience.
Beyond lignite, minerals such as bauxite, silica sand and uorspar provide opportunities to diversify revenue streams and deepen customer 
engagement. The Company's focus is increasingly directed towards quality assurance, grade consistency, application-based marketing 
and value optimisation, enabling these mineral businesses to contribute more meaningfully to long-term earnings growth.
Looking further ahead, opportunities in copper, rare earth elements and other critical minerals represent an important strategic growth 
platform. Progress made during the year through the Ambaji Copper Project, rare earth initiatives, technology collaborations and knowledge 
partnerships reects GMDC’s commitment to building capabilities in mineral segments that are critical to energy transition, advanced 
manufacturing and national resource security. These opportunities are expected to be pursued through a phased and disciplined approach 
that balances growth potential with technical, regulatory and commercial considerations.
A supportive policy environment further strengthens the long-term outlook. Ongoing reforms relating to mine development, resource 
management, digital exploration, coal sector modernisation and energy transition initiatives are creating new opportunities for responsible 
resource development. Leveraging its strong resource base, operational experience and government-backed institutional strengths, GMDC 
is well positioned to participate in these opportunities and create sustainable value for stakeholders over the long term.
Outlook
Looking ahead, GMDC's growth trajectory will be shaped by its ability to convert a diversied resource portfolio into sustainable and 
customer-linked businesses across lignite, coal, bauxite, silica sand, uorspar, limestone, copper, rare earth elements and renewable 
energy opportunities. The pace of this transformation will depend on timely project execution, statutory approvals, mine-readiness, 
environmental stewardship, technology validation, partner collaboration and market development.
In the near term, the Company's priority remains strengthening the core lignite business through reliable mine availability, quality assurance, 
customer engagement and logistics exibility. Alongside lignite, minerals such as bauxite, silica sand and uorspar offer opportunities for 
value enhancement through improved grade consistency, wider market access and application-specic customer solutions. Longer-
gestation opportunities in Odisha coal, limestone, copper and rare earth elements are expected to progress through a phased approach, 
with milestones linked to approvals, infrastructure development, technology choices and capital deployment.

Over the medium term, GMDC's risk and opportunity framework is expected to be increasingly integrated across operating assets, growth 
projects and emerging mineral businesses. While operational priorities will focus on mine productivity, despatch reliability, customer 
retention and performance improvement at Akrimota Thermal Power Station (LTPS), project development efforts will continue to emphasise 
land acquisition, regulatory clearances, stakeholder engagement and execution-readiness. In strategic minerals, progress will depend on 
exploration success, beneciation capabilities, technology partnerships, market qualication and responsible resource development 
practices.
The Company is also strengthening organisational resilience through enhanced governance and risk management practices. The 
implementation of a Business Continuity Plan (BCP) framework and the progressive digitisation of Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) 
processes are expected to improve risk visibility, response preparedness and decision-making effectiveness across business functions. 
These initiatives support proactive management of operational, project, technology and market-related risks in an increasingly dynamic 
business environment.
Digital systems, quality assurance, safety management, compliance frameworks and environmental planning will continue to provide the 
foundation for sustainable growth. By balancing earnings from its established businesses with long-term opportunities in new mines, 
strategic minerals and energy projects, GMDC aims to create enduring value while supporting Gujarat's industrial development and India's 
resource security objectives.
Internal Control and Adequacy
The internal control framework continues to support GMDC’s expanding portfolio of mines, energy assets and strategic growth projects, the 
Company continues to strengthen its internal control framework to support efcient execution and responsible governance. Built on a 
foundation of structured oversight, dened responsibilities and technology-enabled controls, the framework helps maintain process 
reliability, transparency and accountability across business functions.
The internal audit process operates through an independent review mechanism, with quarterly audit coverage placed before the Audit 
Committee. The Committee is chaired by an Independent Director, and internal auditors present observations directly to the Committee, 
covering control design, compliance status and agreed corrective actions. The follow-up mechanism includes review of action-point closure 
in subsequent meetings, creating a clear review trail and audit discipline.
During the year, audit observations led to specic actions, including development of a Bank Guarantee module, recovery of old outstanding 
amounts from BLTPS, and department-based accounting changes in ERP. These examples indicate that the control process is linked not 
only to review, but also to corrective action and process renement.
Financial proposals are subject to pre-audit review before approval, supported by maker-checker controls, payment validations and 
departmental scrutiny. Budgetary controls provide visibility on quarterly and annual expenditure, while major outlays are assessed through 
approved authority levels and internal review processes. As a Government company, the external assurance environment also includes 
audit by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India, including supplementary and propriety audit coverage.
The internal nancial control framework covers xed assets, payroll, entity-level controls, cash and treasury, inventory, intangible assets, 
revenue and receivables, nancial statement closure, purchases and payables, departmental pre-audit and internal audit. Physical 
verication of assets through professional agencies and Chartered Accountants adds another layer of assurance over asset existence and 
record accuracy.
As the operating base widens, control priorities are likely to place greater emphasis on project governance, capital expenditure tracking, 
statutory approvals, vendor performance, digital access controls and data integrity. The framework is positioned to guide growth with 
process reliability, timely oversight and accountability across functions.
e-Governance
Digital governance is embedded across sales, despatch, nance and accounts, material management, internal administration and 
customer interface processes. ERP-based workows, audit trails, e-Sarkar le processing, digital payments and online customer platforms 
provide a more traceable operating environment across the corporate ofce and project locations.
Customer-facing digital processes gained greater commercial relevance during the year. The achievements update records a 100% 
digitised sales process, transition of more than 700 customers to the online portal, 2,680 customers surveyed through market scanning, 
1,757 active customers and more than 4,000 customer visits. These initiatives point to a more structured sales interface, where customer 
data, booking behaviour and eld engagement are becoming part of operating decisions.
Digitalisation also enabled more transparent customer servicing. Online and faceless customer registration, CRM use, digital ledgers and 
customer mapping help align booking, payment, despatch and reconciliation. The broader digital architecture described in the business 
excellence submission includes ERP on cloud, BI dashboards, automated weighbridge systems, LIMS, eet-monitoring tools and digital 
customer platforms. These systems provide visibility across mines, despatch, quality, nance and customer-facing teams, with outcomes 
linked to faster coordination, cleaner transaction trails and more informed customer engagement.
Information security and system continuity are also part of the digital governance agenda. The cyber control framework includes rewalls 
across project locations, advanced email security, web application rewall, sandbox scanning of le uploads, OCI Cloud Guard, EDR/XDR, 
CASB, MDM, patch tracking, half-yearly VAPT, centralised log monitoring, phishing simulations and disaster recovery drills. This gives the 
digital environment a structured control base as operational and commercial processes become more data-led.
The next phase of digital governance is likely to depend on integration, data quality and user discipline. Dashboards, CRM, online booking, 
ERP, customer platforms and quality systems are useful when they provide reliable information for coordination across mines, sales, 
nance, procurement, power and project teams. The focus is therefore on converting digital systems into measurable operating outcomes 
across productivity, customer servicing, grade assurance, safety oversight and decision support.Enabling Billion Dreams of Viksit Bharat

Human Resource and Industrial Relations
GMDC’s people agenda is closely aligned with its evolving business portfolio spanning new mines, strategic minerals, energy projects and 
digital operations. As the Company advances growth initiatives across multiple sectors, capability requirements are becoming increasingly 
specialised, creating demand for skills in mining, geology, project planning, mineral processing, digital technologies, sustainability, safety 
and stakeholder management.
To support this transformation, GMDC continues to strengthen its people framework through the “Rising HR” initiative, anchored on ve 
pillars – digitisation and automation, talent and capability development, employee experience and culture, data-driven HR and governance. 
The programme supports the Company's shift towards a more agile, technology-enabled and project-oriented organisation.
Leadership and talent development remained key focus areas during the year. Project DISHA contributed to capability building through 
cross-functional collaboration in the modernisation and efciency enhancement of the Akrimota Thermal Power Station, while Project 
SHIKHAR focussed on developing leadership capabilities, fostering innovation and strengthening organisational alignment with GMDC’s 
long-term growth vision. Complementing these initiatives, the Young Leaders Programme (YLP) continued to attract and nurture high-
potential talent across mining, engineering, geology, environment and business functions, helping build a future-ready leadership pipeline.
GMDC continued to strengthen workforce capability through online training programmes, webinars, e-learning modules and video-based 
learning sessions covering safety, statutory compliance, cyber awareness, POSH, workplace ethics, mining technologies, environmental 
management and emerging business, ESG and regulatory developments. These initiatives support continuous learning across corporate 
and project locations while enhancing role-specic capabilities in operations, digital adoption, quality, safety and stakeholder management.
Security capability also received focussed attention. During the year, the Security Department undertook welfare activities for security 
personnel, quarterly community welfare programmes through selected project security teams, the rst Security Stakeholders Conclave with 
participation from around 15 security agencies, induction training for 21 newly recruited ex-servicemen supervisors, professional training for 
25 security ofcials at Rashtriya Raksha University, and an internship programme through which 27 students received exposure to industrial 
and corporate security practices. These initiatives add a practical layer to site preparedness, contractor interface, asset protection and 
community-linked security awareness.
Renewable energy initiatives also reect the need for cross-functional capability. The RE Department progressed conductor and earth wire 
replacement for the 66 kV Madhavpur-Gorsar transmission line, formation of an SPV with GACL for a hybrid renewable energy project, 
installation of climbing systems at 67 wind turbines, rooftop solar proposals at Bhavnagar and Mevasa, optimisation planning for the 5 MW 
Panandhro solar plant, and feasibility assessment for solar and wind projects at Gadhsisa. These initiatives require coordination across 
technical, nance, procurement, legal, project and site teams, showing how energy opportunities depend as much on cross-functional 
readiness as on asset availability.
As the asset base expands across Gujarat and Odisha, the people agenda is likely to place greater emphasis on workforce-readiness, 
safety behaviour, contractor interface, local engagement and capability building for project-intensive operations. Industrial relations are 
therefore expected to draw on structured engagement, dened HR processes, welfare measures, training, grievance channels and site-
level coordination. The overall direction is to align people systems with the needs of a mining and energy enterprise that is becoming more 
technology-enabled, customer-oriented and project-led while retaining workplace continuity across operating locations.
Way Forward
The business outlook is centred on converting the resource base of GMDC into a more customer-linked, quality-led and project-ready 
minerals and energy enterprise. In the near term, lignite stays central, with revenue conversion shaped by mine-readiness, exposed lignite 
availability, despatch reliability, grade consistency and closer customer engagement. This earnings base provides the nancial foundation 
for wider mineral and energy priorities.
Beyond lignite, bauxite, silica sand and uorspar provide a broader commercial base, with business potential linked to grade consistency, 
beneciation, customer-specic applications and market-based price discovery. New lignite mines, Odisha coal blocks, copper, limestone 
and rare earth initiatives dene the medium-term growth agenda, subject to approvals, technical validation, infrastructure, partner timelines 
and market linkage. Across these opportunities, the priority is to move from resource access to permitted, quality-assured and customer-
linked businesses.
Strategic minerals and energy options add a longer-term pathway. Copper, rare earths, critical mineral intelligence, renewables and 
gasication place the Company within resource security priorities for India and the energy transition agenda. Progress is likely to follow a 
phased and commercially measured approach, relying on partnerships, technology validation, processing capability and careful capital 
phasing rather than rapid expansion alone.
Digital systems, grade assurance, governance, internal controls and people capability provide the operating base for this next phase. The 
overall direction is to balance earnings from existing businesses with carefully sequenced growth in new minerals and energy options, while 
focussing on dependable supply, customer condence, responsible mining and long-term business contribution aligned with Gujarat 
industrial requirements and resource security priorities for India.

1. Brief outline on CSR Policy of the Company
Believing and practising a culture of responsible development, GMDC has introduced its Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) Policy and 
activities in accordance with the Companies Act, 2013, Companies (Corporate Social Responsibility) Rules, 2014 and CSR Amendment 
Rules, 2021, notied on 22 January, 2021 (Notication No. G.S.R. 40 (E). The vision and mission of GMDC is to improve the quality of life and 
empower the communities in the working and surrounding areas of GMDC. 
GMDC strategically operates in a complex ecosystem to implement various social development projects in the thrust areas of Skill 
Ecosystem, Promotion of Quality and Inclusive Education, Health, drinking water and Sanitation, Ensuring Climate Action, and 
Environmental Sustainability with a responsibility of improvement of quality of life and holistic development of surrounding communities. 
The objectives of the CSR policy of GMDC are as below: 
• To provide a robust framework for carrying out the CSR initiatives in alignment with Companies (Corporate Social Responsibility Policy) 
Amendment Rules, 2021 notied on 22 January, 2021 (Notication No. G.S.R. 40 (E) (Ensure increased commitment at all levels in the 
organisation to operate its business economically, socially & environmentally sustainable manner while recognising the interests of all 
its stakeholders).
• To bring about tangible socio-economic development in CORE, BUFFER & EMERGING ZONES  of GMDC, thereby improving the local 
community’s well-being through discretionary business practices and contribution of corporate resources;
• To emerge as a responsible corporate leader in Sustainable CSR Initiatives through innovative partnerships/programmes, strategic 
collaborations, and stakeholder engagement to promote inclusive community growth.
The CSR projects of GMDC are implemented directly by GMDC or through GMDC-Gramya Vikas Trust (CSR Implementing Agency of 
GMDC), or through NGOs/Civil Society Organisations/Trust, or through concerned District Authorities/Panchayati Raj Institutions at 
District/Block/Village Level. The primary participants of these projects include children, youth, women, and community members. 
Monitoring and Evaluation (M&E) are integral part of Program preparation and implementation. Accordingly, GMDC has developed a 
Monitoring and Evaluation framework ensuring transparency and accountability with well-dened Outputs, Outcomes and Impact for the 
Actions taken under project implementation. 
GMDC CSR policy is aligned with the national priorities, sustainable development goals and Gujarat State Vision. It would hence be 
interweaving all the development indicators and work towards Sustainable Development Goals.
